Sunpower Corp. v. Solarcity Corp.

United States District Court for the Northern District of California, 2012  
[2012 WL 6160472, at \*1–16](http://lawschool.westlaw.com/shared/westlawRedirect.aspx?task=find&cite=2012+WL+6160472&appflag=67.12)

Lucy H. Koh, District Judge.

Before the Court is Defendants SolarCity Corporation, Tom Leyden, Matt Giannini, Dan Leary, Felix Aguayo, and Alice Catchart’s (“Defendants”) Partial Motion to Dismiss. Having considered the parties’ submissions and the relevant case law, and the parties’ arguments at the hearing held on November 8, 2012, the Court GRANTS Defendants’ Motion.

I.FACTUAL BACKGROUND

SunPower is a leading manufacturer and distributor of high-efficiency solar panels and other related equipment. SolarCity is a distributor of solar panels and other related equipment. Defendants Tom Leyden, Matt Giannini, Dan Leary, Felix Aguayo, and Alice Cathcart (the “Individual Defendants”) were employed by SunPower in sales positions before being recruited by SolarCity. Each of the Individual Defendants signed agreements at SunPower agreeing not to disclose “confidential or proprietary information” to third parties and to return such information to SunPower upon ending their employment.

On or about December 9, 2011, SunPower discovered that Aguayo had accessed his company email account after he was terminated. SunPower also discovered that Aguayo had forwarded several emails containing customer information, price lists, and market reports to his personal email address on or about November 18, 2011. Based on the emails Aguayo accessed and the proximity in time to Leyden, Giannini, Leary, Aguayo, and Catchart’s departures, SunPower initiated an investigation, including conducting a computer forensic analysis of the computers used by the Individual Defendants.

SunPower’s investigation revealed that, shortly before leaving SunPower, each of the Individual Defendants had used various means, including USB devices and portable hard drives, to store SunPower files containing “confidential . . . and non-confidential proprietary information.” This information consisted of, inter alia, contact information, sales histories, potential new sales, status, market and business analysis, quotes, forecast analysis, cash flow analysis, and project economics. SunPower is informed and believes that this information has been delivered to Defendant 195SolarCity and that Defendants “continue to use . . . \[the\] data . . . for their own benefit.”

II.PROCEDURAL BACKGROUND

As a result of Defendants’ actions, on February 13, 2012, SunPower filed the instant action. In this action, SunPower alleges that Defendants misappropriated SunPower’s trade secrets in violation of the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, Cal. Civ.Code § 3426 et seq. (“Trade Secrets Claim”). In addition to SunPower’s Trade Secrets Claim, SunPower alleges several causes of action based on Defendant’s misappropriation of what SunPower terms “nontrade secret proprietary information.” These causes of action include SunPower’s: (1) fourth cause of action for breach of confidence, (2) fifth cause of action for conversion, (3) sixth cause of action for trespass to chattels, (4) seventh cause of action for tortious interference with prospective economic advantage; (5) eighth cause of action for common law unfair competition; and (6) ninth cause of action for unfair competition under California Business & Professions Code section 17200 (collectively, “Non-Trade Secret Claims”).

On August 2, 2012, Defendants filed the instant Motion seeking dismissal of SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims. Defendants’ primary basis for relief is that the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act supersedes SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims.

\* \* \*

IV.DISCUSSION

In the instant Motion, Defendants move to dismiss the Non-Trade Secret Claims on the grounds that: (1) California law has never recognized causes of action for conversion, trespass to chattels, tortious interference with prospective economic advantage, common-law unfair competition, or statutory unfair competition based on the misappropriation of “non-trade secret proprietary information”; and (2) even if California law did previously allow such claims, such claims are now superseded by the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (“CUTSA”). Defendants also argue that SunPower’s seventh cause of action for tortious interference with prospective economic advantage should be dismissed because SunPower has failed to allege that Defendants’ conduct interfered with SunPower’s relationship with a specific third party. The Court addresses the supersession issue first and concludes that SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims are superseded.

A.CUTSA Supersession

1.Background on CUTSA and CUTSA Supersession

California’s Uniform Trade Secrets Act provides for the civil recovery of “actual loss” or other injury caused by the misappropriation of trade 196secrets. Cal. Civ.Code § 3426.3. Misappropriation means improper acquisition, or non-consensual disclosure or use of another’s trade secret. Id. § 3426.1(b). The statute defines a “trade secret” as information that derives “independent economic value” from its confidentiality and “\[i\]s the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy.”

CUTSA includes a savings clause (Section 3426.7) that “preempt\[s\] claims based on the same nucleus of facts as trade secret misappropriation.” The savings clause does not affect “contractual remedies” and civil remedies “that are not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret.” Silvaco Data Systems v. Intel Corp., 184 Cal.App.4th 236 (2010). “The preemption inquiry for those causes of action not specifically exempted by § 3426.7(b) focuses on whether other claims are not more than a restatement of the same operative facts supporting trade secret misappropriation . . . If there is no material distinction between the wrongdoing alleged in a\[C\]UTSA claim and that alleged in a different claim, the \[C\]UTSA claim preempts the other claim.” Convolve, Inc. v. Compaq Comp. Corp, 2006 WL 839022 (S.D.N.Y. 2006).

Following the nucleus of facts test, a number of Courts, including this Court, have held that CUTSA may supersede various claims including, inter alia, claims for conversion, common count, quantum meruit, unjust enrichment, breach of confidence, unfair competition, and intentional and negligent misrepresentation where the wrongdoing alleged in connection with such claims is the misappropriation of trade secrets. \* \* \*

2.CUTSA Can Supersede Claims Based on the Misappropriation of Non-Trade Secret Information

In this case, SunPower does not dispute that the UTSA supersedes common-law claims to the extent such claims “are based on the same nucleus of facts as the misappropriation of trade secrets claim for relief.” Rather, SunPower argues that its Non-Trade Secret Claims are not based on the same nucleus of fact as its Trade Secret Claim because the Non-Trade Secret Claims relate to the misappropriation of SunPower’s non-trade secret proprietary information, as opposed to the misappropriation of SunPower’s trade secrets. Thus, the Court must determine whether a claim based on the misappropriation of non-trade secret proprietary information is superseded by CUTSA.

Only one California Court has explicitly considered this issue, specifically the California Court of Appeal in Silvaco. The Silvaco Court held that the UTSA superseded claims for conversion, common count, common law unfair business practices, and intentional and negligent misrepresentation because those claims were based on the misappropriation of trade secrets plaintiff claimed were “contained” in computer software it had developed. In a footnote addressing the Eastern District of Pennsylvania’s decision in 197Cenveo Corp. v. Slater, 2007 WL 527720 (E.D.Pa. 2007), the Silvaco Court stated:

We emphatically reject the Cenveo court’s suggestion that the uniform act was not intended to preempt “common law conversion claims based on the taking of information that, though not a trade secret, was nonetheless of value to the claimant.” On the contrary, a prime purpose of the law was to sweep away the adopting states’ bewildering web of rules and rationales and replace it with a uniform set of principles for determining when one is—and is not—liable for acquiring, disclosing, or using “information . . . of value.” Central to the effort was the act’s definition of a trade secret. Information that does not fit this definition, and is not otherwise made property by some provision of positive law, belongs to no one, and cannot be converted or stolen. By permitting the conversion claim to proceed on a contrary rationale, the Cenveo court impliedly created a new category of intellectual property far beyond the contemplation of the Act, subsuming its definition of “trade secret” and effectively obliterating the uniform system it seeks to generate.

Defendants contend that the Silvaco footnote stands for the proposition that, under California law, SunPower’s claims based on the misappropriation of non\-trade secret proprietary information are superseded. The Court agrees that this footnote supports Defendants’ argument. However, the Court notes that an argument could be made that the footnote is dicta as, unlike in the instant case, in Silvaco, there does not actually appear to have been any allegation by plaintiff that the information plaintiff was seeking to protect was not a trade secret and therefore not subject to trade secret law.

Nevertheless, even if the statement in Silvaco is technically dicta, given the Silvaco Court’s “emphatic\[ \]” rejection of SunPower’s position, absent “convincing evidence that” the California Supreme Court “would decide \[this issue\] differently,” this Court believes it prudent to follow Silvaco. Here, SunPower has not identified any decision that suggests the California Supreme Court would conclude that CUTSA does not supersede claims based on the misappropriation of confidential or proprietary information that nevertheless fails to qualify as a trade secret under CUTSA.

Moreover, the Court agrees with the rationale in Silvaco. In order for the taking of information to constitute wrongdoing, the information must be property. Information is not property unless some “positive law” makes it so. Thus, the Court agrees with the Silvaco Court that, in order to state a claim based on the taking of information, a plaintiff must show that he has some property right in such information (i.e. that the information is 198proprietary). If the basis of the alleged property right is in essence that the information is that it is “not . . . generally known to the public,” then the claim is sufficiently close to a trade secret claim that it should be superseded notwithstanding the fact that the information fails to meet the definition of a trade secret. To permit otherwise would allow plaintiffs to avoid the preclusive effect of CUTSA (and thereby plead potentially more favorable common-law claims) by simply failing to allege one of the elements necessary for information to qualify as a trade secret. For example, a Plaintiff seeking to bring a non-CUTSA claim based on the misappropriation of valuable information could avoid supersession under CUTSA by failing to allege that the information was “subject” to “reasonable” efforts “to maintain its secrecy.” Such a result would subvert CUTSA’s purpose of providing a “uniform set of principles for determining when one is—and is not—liable for acquiring, disclosing, or using ‘information . . . of value.’ ”

\* \* \*

In light of Silvaco, the Court concludes that SunPower’s claims based on its non-trade secret proprietary information are superseded unless one of the following conditions is met: (1) SunPower can allege facts that show that “the \[non-trade secret proprietary\] information . . . was ‘made property by some provision of positive law,’ . . . on grounds that are qualitatively different from the grounds upon which trade secrets are considered property,” or (2) it can otherwise be concluded that SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims allege “wrongdoing” that is “material\[ly\] distinct\[ \] \[from\] the wrongdoing alleged in a\[C\]UTSA claim. . . .” The Court addresses each of these issues in turn.

3.SunPower Has Not Alleged Facts Sufficient to Show That SunPower Has a Property Interest in its Non-Trade Secret Proprietary Information

Having reviewed the Complaint, the Court concludes that, notwithstanding SunPower’s labeling of its non-trade secret information as “proprietary,” SunPower has failed to allege facts sufficient to show that SunPower has property rights in its non-trade secret information.

As an initial matter, SunPower never actually defines the term “non-trade secret proprietary information.” Indeed, the term does not appear anywhere in the section of SunPower’s Complaint setting forth SunPower’s factual allegations regarding Defendants’ alleged misconduct. The term does not make its first appearance until the portions of SunPower’s Complaint setting forth its specific causes of action. No information is provided in these sections regarding what information SunPower contends constitutes non-trade secret proprietary information. Given the dearth of information concerning the nature of SunPower’s non-trade secret 199proprietary information, the Court cannot conclude that this information is made property by virtue of some law other than CUTSA.

The Court also notes that, in the section of SunPower’s Complaint setting forth its factual allegations regarding Defendants’ alleged misconduct, SunPower uses the terms “confidential information” and “non-confidential proprietary information.” While SunPower makes a facial distinction between these two categories, SunPower uses both terms to refer to the same computer files. See e.g. ¶ 34 (alleging that Defendants stole “tens-of thousands of computer files containing \[SunPower\] confidential information and non-confidential proprietary information . . . \[and that these\] files included . . . quotes, deals, proposals, contracts, and files containing forecast analysis, market analysis, business analysis and information downloaded” from SunPower’s sales website); id. ¶ 36 (alleging that Leyden “copied at least thousands of files containing \[SunPower\] confidential information and non-confidential proprietary information . . . include\[ing\] hundreds of quotes, proposals, and contracts, as well as files containing market analysis, forecast analysis, and business analysis”); id. ¶ 41 (alleging that Leary “copied at least tens-of-thousands of files containing \[SunPower\] confidential information and non-confidential proprietary information . . . \[including\] over 40,000 quotes, contracts, proposals and deals . . .,” etc . . .).

SunPower’s use of the terms “confidential information” and “non-confidential proprietary information” to refer to the same data without making any effort to assign particular data to particular categories suggests that the distinction SunPower is drawing is superficial. To the extent SunPower uses the terms “confidential information” and “non-confidential proprietary information” as proxies for the terms “trade secret information” and “non-trade secret proprietary information,” the Court concludes that the distinction SunPower draws between the latter two categories of information is likely superficial as well. Thus, the Complaint supports the conclusion that any property interest SunPower may have in its non-trade secret proprietary information is qualitatively no different from the grounds upon which its trade secrets are considered property. Accordingly, the Court cannot conclude from these facts that SunPower has a property interest in the non-trade secret proprietary information or that this property interest is sufficiently distinct from its interest in its trade secrets such that its Non-Trade Secret Claims are not superseded.

Notwithstanding SunPower’s failure to allege what information constitutes non-trade secret proprietary information, in its Opposition, SunPower argues that “California law clearly recognizes a property right in” its non-trade secret. Accordingly, SunPower contends that its Non-Trade Secret Claims should not be superseded. The Court is not persuaded. SunPower fails to support its arguments with any case law recognizing a broad property right in non-trade secret proprietary information. SunPower does 200cite to several cases, in which Courts allowed claims for conversion, trespass to chattels, and common law unfair competition to proceed based on the misappropriation of intangible property, but these cases fail to support the conclusion that the nontrade secret proprietary information at issue here is property.

For example, SunPower cites the Ninth Circuit’s decision in Kremen v. Cohen, 337 F.3d 1024 (9th Cir. 2003). In Kremen, after applying a three-part test, the Court concluded that the owner of a website domain name had a property right in the domain name and could therefore pursue a claim for conversion based on the Defendant’s sale of the domain name to another party. Kremen’s recognition that plaintiff had a property right in the domain name does not support the broad proposition that “California law . . . recognizes a property right in” non-trade secret information.

Moreover, Kremen’s conclusion that the domain name was property was based in part on its finding that the plaintiff had a “legitimate claim to exclusivity” as to the domain name. Here, one of the issues with SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims is that SunPower has failed to provide sufficient information for the Court to conclude that: (1) SunPower has a “legitimate claim to exclusivity” in the non-trade secret information, and (2) SunPower’s basis for claiming an exclusive right to such information is different from the grounds upon which the information might be deemed a trade secret under CUTSA.

SunPower also cites Thrifty-Tel, Inc. v. Bezenek. Thrifty-Tel, 46 Cal.App.4th 1559 (1996), held that a jury could have properly found defendants guilty of trespass to a chattel where defendants “employed computer technology in their efforts to crack plaintiff’s access and authorization codes and make long distance phone calls without paying for them . . .” Thrifty-Tel does not stand for the broad proposition that SunPower has a property interest in all non-trade secret proprietary information. The holding in Thrifty-Tell might be read as acknowledging that plaintiff had some property rights with respect to the “confidential codes” used to gain access to plaintiff’s computer systems. However, to the extent the opinion in Thrifty-Tell suggests that plaintiff had a property interest in the access codes, this property interest was based on the codes “confidential” nature; thus, the relevant property interest was qualitatively the same as an individual’s interest in trade secret information. As set forth in Silvaco, a claim based on the misappropriation of confidential information would certainly be superseded by CUTSA. Significantly, Thrifty-Tell was decided in 1996, fourteen years before Silvaco, and the Thrifty-Tell Court never considered CUTSA or whether plaintiff’s claims were superseded by CUTSA.

Likewise, SunPower’s citations to City Solutions and Imax are also unavailing. In Imax and City Solutions, the Ninth Circuit held that the 201plaintiffs in those cases could proceed on theories of common law misappropriation, notwithstanding the fact that they were unable to prevail on their trade secret claims. One of the elements of a common-law misappropriation claim is that SunPower has “invested substantial time and money in \[the\] development of its property.” It could be argued that the doctrine of common law misappropriation therefore establishes a property right of sorts in the information that a party has “invested substantial time and money in” developing. However, SunPower has not alleged any facts regarding what the non-trade secret information is, much less facts showing SunPower invested substantial time and money in developing this information. Thus, even assuming a common law misappropriation claim could be maintained (i.e. that such a claim is not superseded by CUTSA), SunPower’s claim would fail. Moreover, even if SunPower had alleged such facts and the Court were to accept the proposition that, pursuant to the doctrine of common law misappropriation, SunPower may have a property interest in information that Plaintiff “invested substantial time and money” in developing, SunPower has failed to identify any case concluding that this property right may support anything other than a common law misappropriation claim (which Plaintiff has not alleged). Thus, Plaintiff’s Non-Trade Secret Claims (which allege conversion, trespass to chattels, etc . . .) would still fail.

4.The Wrongdoing Alleged in SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims Is Not Different from the Wrongdoing Alleged in SunPower’s Trade Secret Claim

SunPower also argues that its Non-Trade Secret Claims are not preempted because they “require \[ \] additional facts and legal requirements apart from the misappropriation of trade secrets” and are therefore based on a different nucleus of fact than SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims. The Court disagrees. As set forth above, the nucleus of fact test does not focus on whether a non-CUTSA claim requires the pleading of different elements than the CUTSA claim, but rather on whether “there is \[a\] material distinction between the wrongdoing alleged in a \[C\]UTSA claim and that alleged in \[the non-CUTSA\] claim. . . .” Here, the Court concludes that there is no material difference between the wrongdoing alleged in support of SunPower’s Trade Secret Claim and the wrongdoing alleged in support of SunPower’s Non Trade Secret Claims.

As an initial matter, the Court notes that SunPower’s Non Trade Secret Claims incorporate the same factual allegations regarding Defendants’ unauthorized access and use of SunPower’s information as SunPower’s Trade Secret Claim. \* \* \*

Furthermore, while stated in various ways, each of SunPower’s Non-Trade Secret Claims alleges in essence that Defendants violated SunPower’s 202rights by acquiring, disclosing, and/or using, without consent (i.e. misappropriating) SunPower’s proprietary information. \* \* \* Accordingly, the Court concludes that the wrongdoing alleged in connection with each of the Non-Trade Secret Claims is in essence the same wrongdoing as was alleged in connection with SunPower’s Trade Secret Claim. The Non-Trade Secret Claims are therefore superseded.

\* \* \*

VI.CONCLUSION

For the foregoing reasons, Defendants’ Partial Motion to Dismiss is GRANTED, with leave to amend . . . . \* \* \*

Questions

1.What common law tort claims are potentially available for the protection of information?

2.What does the court say is the purpose behind the “supersession” provision (referred to as a preemption or preclusion provision in other jurisdictions) in California’s version of the UTSA?

3.How does the court characterize information? Is all of it protectable, or just some?

4.If only some information is protectable, how do we tell which information is protectable and which is not? Does information have to be tangible to be protected?

F.Statutory Law

Given the above limits of common law tort theories for the protection of information, legislatures can choose to adopt statutes that either broaden the protections that are available at common law or create new statutory torts, provided the state statutes are not preempted by federal law. When they do so, however, they should confront the public interest in information diffusion, including related First Amendment concerns, and determine whether the benefits of such laws outweigh the detriments.

Trade secret law is an example of a tort theory of recovery that developed at common law and was later altered pursuant to statute, both under the UTSA and the DTSA. While the UTSA limited the common law of trade secrecy in several ways, it broadened it by: providing protection for so-called “negative information;” expanding the available remedies; and defining “actual harm” more broadly than was recognized at common law. See Sharon K. Sandeen, The Evolution of Trade Secret Law and Why Courts Commit Error When They Do Not Follow the UTSA, 33 Hamline L. Rev. 493 (2010). But as noted above, trade secret laws cannot be written or applied so broadly that they interfere with the purposes of U.S. patent and 203copyright law, including what those laws say about the types of information that cannot be protected.

Copyright law is an example of a statute that created a new tort, although analogous concepts had developed at common law and so-called “common law copyright” principles continue to exist in some states. But it is important to understand that copyright law was not designed to protect information per se; rather, it was designed to incentivize the creation of works of authorship by creating exclusive rights that are limited in both scope and time. Moreover, like patent law, U.S. copyright law reflects an important disclosure or “public access” purpose that should not be impinged by state law. See Diane L. Zimmerman, Trade Secrets and the ‘Philosophy’ of Copyright: A Case of Culture Crash, in The Law and Theory of Trade Secrecy (Rochelle C. Dreyfuss and Katherine J. Strandburg, eds., Edward Elgar 2011) (noting that: “Copyright. . . was designed as a system of incentives to encourage authors to make their work publicly available”).

Since the advent of computers and concomitant concerns related to computer hacking, perhaps the most important statute to be enacted related to the protection of information is the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA), which is discussed in the case that follows and in Chapter 7. Other examples include information privacy laws, some of which are discussed in Chapter 6, including the European Union General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and the European Union Database Directive which provides limited protection for qualifying databases.

When representing a client like the one that is described at the beginning of this chapter, research must be conducted to determine the full-array of common law and statutory information torts that are recognized in the relevant jurisdictions. These torts may be industry or information specific and, as discussed previously, some of them may be precluded or preempted.

State Analysis, Inc. v. American Financial Services Assoc.

 

United States District Court, E.D. Virginia, 2009  
[621 F.Supp.2d 309](http://lawschool.westlaw.com/shared/westlawRedirect.aspx?task=find&cite=621+F.Supp.2d+309&appflag=67.12)

Leonie M. Brinkema, District Judge.

The defendants have moved to dismiss several of the counts of the Complaint for failure to state a claim. For the reasons stated in open court and in this opinion, the defendants’ motions will be granted in part and denied in part.

204 

I.Background

Plaintiff State Analysis, Inc. d/b/a/ StateScape (“StateScape”) is a Virginia government relations and analysis firm that owns and operates a searchable, proprietary database of local, state, and federal bills and regulations, and sells access to it on a subscription basis to its clients. It claims to be the first firm to offer tracking of state legislation and regulation, and has been in business since 1991. According to the Complaint, StateScape’s software downloads bills and regulations from government websites, and its analysts then examine the bills, “tag” them according to issue areas, and put together customized listings of bills and regulations for StateScape’s customers.

Co-defendant American Financial Services Association (“AFSA”) is a business association headquartered in Washington, D.C. whose members are financial services companies. AFSA was a client of StateScape from 1998 through 2008 under a series of renewed one-year contracts. Under the terms of AFSA’s contracts with StateScape, businesses that were members of AFSA were provided with access to StateScape’s database and custom reports, and each AFSA member received a StateScape username and password.

Co-defendant Kimbell Sherman Ellis (“KSE”) is a government relations and public affairs firm located in Montpelier, Vermont whose services include monitoring legislative and regulatory developments. KSE was a customer of StateScape between March 1, 1999 and February 29, 2000; however, it is now a competitor of StateScape.

In December 2002, KSE offered to purchase StateScape’s database. StateScape declined the offer and shortly thereafter fired its marketing director, co-defendant Leif Johnson. Johnson was subject to a non-compete and non-disclosure agreement that prohibited him, for one year from the date his employment with StateScape ended, from working for any entity or service similar to the services he performed for StateScape, and from performing similar services for any StateScape customer. Notwithstanding these agreements, Johnson was hired by KSE in or about July 2003 and began working in KSE’s Washington office. KSE also hired at least one other StateScape employee, researcher Gia Biden, who had done research services for StateScape’s contract with AFSA. Biden began working for KSE sometime after August 13, 2003.

On October 23, 2008, AFSA informed StateScape that it would not renew its contract and planned to switch to KSE’s tracking database, FOCUS, beginning on January 1, 2009. StateScape claims it was surprised because AFSA had never complained to StateScape about its services or costs. StateScape began to investigate AFSA’s activity logs in its database, and discovered that from October 2004 through November 2008, the database had been accessed 735 times from an internet protocol (“IP”) address 205located in Montpelier, Vermont—the location of KSE’s headquarters—using three usernames associated with AFSA employees who worked in AFSA’s Washington office. According to the Complaint, KSE is not, and never has been, a member of AFSA.

StateScape further discovered, on AFSA’s website, a number of “white papers . . . prepared for AFSA by KSE containing bill summaries markedly similar, if not identical, to those authored by StateScape.” In those white papers, it discovered “bill counts”—listings of the number of bills reported to exist on a topic—that were identical to the bill counts for subjects using the StateScape database. StateScape also discovered, on KSE’s website, that a number of features of StateScape’s proprietary database had been incorporated into KSE’s FOCUS database.

StateScape concluded that KSE repeatedly accessed StateScape’s database from 2004 through 2008, using usernames and passwords provided to KSE by AFSA, and downloaded and copied StateScape database records, including copyrighted works. On November 13, 2008, StateScape temporarily blocked AFSA’s passwords and reminded AFSA of its obligations not to share its passwords and usernames with unauthorized persons. It also blocked access to its database from the Vermont IP address. One week later, after receiving a response from AFSA, StateScape reactivated the passwords but has continued to block access from the Vermont IP address.

\[Authors’ note: As is typical of many complaints in information related cases, StateScape’s Complaint included numerous causes of action (eleven in total), including claims for: copyright infringement; violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA); violation of the Electronic Communications Privacy Act; violation of the Virginia Computer Crimes Act; misappropriation of trade secrets; breach of contract; trespass to chattels; unjust enrichment; interference with prospective economic relations; and interference with contract. The following has been edited to include only the court’s discussion of the CFAA and the analogous Virginia statute.\]

\* \* \*

III.Discussion

A.Count 2: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act.

StateScape has alleged that AFSA and KSE have violated two distinct provisions of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (“CFAA”), 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) and 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(6).

 

18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2) prohibits “intentionally access\[ing\] a computer without authorization or exceed\[ing\] authorized access, and thereby obtain \[ing\] . . . information from any protected computer . . .” “Exceeds authorized access” is explicitly defined as “to access a computer with authorization and 206to use such access to obtain or alter Information in the computer that the accesser is not entitled so to obtain or alter.” 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(6). Both AFSA and KSE have moved to dismiss this count on the grounds that they did not access StateScape’s systems “without authorization” or “exceed authorized access.”

Courts have differed as to how broadly or narrowly to construe 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(2). Some authorities have held that the CFAA was targeted at “computer hackers (e.g., electronic trespassers),” and only applies to a situation “where an outsider, or someone without authorization, accesses a computer.” These authorities have rejected attempts to apply the CFAA to cases where the defendants are not alleged to have “broken into” the system but to have abused the privileges of a license. Other courts have held that the CFAA does apply to authorized users who use programs in an unauthorized way, including employees who obtain and use proprietary information in violation of a duty of loyalty, and licensees who breach an agreement restricting their use of the software. Taking these authorities into account, on the facts alleged in the Complaint, the Court finds that StateScape has stated a claim under § 1030(a)(2) against KSE, but not against AFSA.

According to the Complaint, KSE accessed StateScape’s website using usernames and passwords that did not belong to it. StateScape has pled that under the terms of their contract, only clients were authorized to use StateScape’s subscription services, and that KSE was not so authorized. KSE therefore acted “without authorization.” KSE may not hide behind purported “authorization” granted to it by AFSA, particularly given that KSE, a former client of StateScape that employed StateScape’s former marketing director, was presumably familiar with the terms of StateScape’s agreement and with the scope of authority granted to licensees.

KSE has also moved for a partial dismissal of the CFAA claims on statute of limitations grounds. A two-year statute of limitations, which begins to run from “the date of the act complained of or the date of discovery of the damage,” applies to this claim. 18 U.S.C. § 1030(g). “Damage” is defined in the CFAA as “any impairment to the integrity or availability of data, a program, a system, or information.” 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(8). KSE correctly argues that StateScape has not pled that it suffered any “damage” as a result of the defendants’ alleged conduct, as it has not alleged that the “integrity or availability of data, a program, a system, or information” has been impaired. The CFAA allows a plaintiff to recover for “loss,” defined as “any reasonable cost to any victim . . .” as well as “damage;” however, it distinguishes between loss and damage in that the “discovery” provision that can lengthen the statute of limitations applies only to the discovery of damage, not loss. Because StateScape has alleged that it has suffered only loss, but not damage, the statute of limitations for the CFAA claim began 207to run from the date of the defendants’ alleged violations and therefore bars any claims for violations occurring before December 24, 2006, two years before the Complaint was filed.

AFSA’s Motion to Dismiss the § 1030(a)(2) claim will be granted. It is undisputed that AFSA itself never went beyond the areas that StateScape authorized AFSA to access. Rather, StateScape alleges that AFSA was “without authorization” because it breached its contract with StateScape in which it agreed to provide access to StateScape’s services only to AFSA members. In its opposition to AFSA’s Motion to Dismiss, StateScape relies on case law holding that employees who use their employers’ computers to pass information to competitors act “without authorization.” See, e.g., Shurgard Storage Centers, Inc. v. Safeguard Self Storage, Inc. (holding that an employee, who by virtue of his employment was authorized to access his employer’s computers, became “without authorization” when he became an “agent” for the defendant, one of his employer’s competitors, to whom he sent e-mails containing his employer’s trade secrets and other proprietary information). These cases, however, are distinguishable because AFSA’s contract with StateScape makes clear that in the event that AFSA breached the contract by providing its passwords to others, StateScape reserved the right to terminate AFSA’s contract, but it was not automatically terminated. As such, at no point was AFSA’s access “without authorization.” AFSA’s alleged offense was not an unauthorized access—which § 1030(a)(2) prohibits-but an unauthorized use or misappropriation.

AFSA’s access also did not “exceed authorization” within the meaning of the CFAA. As explained supra, the CFAA explicitly defines “exceeds authorization” as “to access a computer with authorization and to use such access to obtain or alter information in the computer that the accesser is not entitled so to obtain or alter.” 18 U.S.C. § 1030(e)(6). Nowhere in the Complaint does StateScape allege that AFSA obtained or altered any information it was not entitled to; rather, the allegation is that AFSA used the information in an inappropriate way. Such allegations do not state a claim for a violation of § 1030(a)(2). Accordingly, AFSA’s motion to dismiss those claims in Count 2 that fall under § 1030(a)(2) will be granted.

StateScape has also sued KSE and AFSA for violations of 18 U.S.C. § 1030(a)(6), which prohibits “knowingly and with intent, to defraud traffic \[king\] (as defined in section 1029) in any password or similar information through which a computer may be accessed without authorization.” Only KSE has moved to dismiss this claim.

 

18 U.S.C. § 1029 defines “traffic” as “transfer, or otherwise dispose of, to another, or obtain control of with intent to transfer or dispose of.” The Complaint does not allege that KSE transferred, or otherwise disposed of, AFSA’s passwords; rather, it alleges that KSE received them from AFSA and used them without authorization. Such conduct does not constitute 208“trafficking” under § 1029. Therefore, KSE’s motion to dismiss the § 1030(a)(6) trafficking claim will be granted.

\* \* \*

C.Count 4: Virginia Computer Crimes Act.

AFSA and KSE have moved to dismiss the Virginia Computer Crimes Act, Va.Code § 18.2–152.3 et seq. (“VCCA”), on multiple grounds, including preemption of the VCCA by the Copyright Act. Section 301(a) of the Copyright Act states:

“all legal or equitable rights that are equivalent to any of the exclusive rights within the general scope of copyright as specified by section 106 \[of the Copyright Act\] in works of authorship that are fixed in a tangible medium of expression and come within the subject matter of copyright as specified by sections 102 and 103 . . . are governed exclusively by this title.”

 

17 U.S.C. § 301(a). A state law claim is preempted by the Copyright Act if (1) the work at issue is “within the scope of the ‘subject matter of copyright’ as specified in 17 U.S.C.A. §§ 102, 103 and (2) the rights granted under state law are equivalent to any exclusive rights within the scope of federal copyright as set out in 17 U.S.C.A. § 106.” Rosciszewski v. Arete Associates, Inc. A right under state law is “equivalent” to a right under federal copyright law if that right “may be abridged by an act which, in and of itself, would infringe one of the exclusive rights \[granted in the Copyright Act\].” Id. “However, if an extra element is required instead of or in addition to the acts of reproduction, performance, distribution or display, in order to constitute a state-created cause of action, there is no preemption . . . provided that the extra element changes the nature of the action so that it is qualitatively different from a copyright infringement claim.” Id. \* \* \*

The elements of a violation of the VCCA are that the defendant (1) uses a computer or computer network; (2) without authority; and (3) either obtains property or services by false pretenses, embezzles or commits larceny; or converts the property of another. Va.Code § 18.2–152.3. In Rosciszewski, the Fourth Circuit held that a claim under a prior, but similar, version of the VCCA based on unauthorized copying of copyrighted software was preempted by the Copyright Act. It concluded that the first element for preemption was satisfied because software is within the subject matter of copyright. It next found that rights granted under the VCCA that protect against unauthorized copying of software are equivalent to those granted by the Copyright Act because none of the three elements of the VCCA were sufficient to “qualitatively chang\[e\] the state claim from one of unauthorized copying.” On these findings, the Fourth Circuit concluded that “the protection of computer programs from unauthorized copying granted under § 18.2–152.3 is equivalent to the exclusive right of the copyright owner to reproduce a copyrighted work under the Copyright Act,” 209and that a cause of action under the VCCA “is preempted to the extent that it is based on reproduction of \[a\] copyrighted computer program.”

Given the Fourth Circuit’s holding, the only basis for finding that the VCCA claim is not preempted would be if the VCCA violations alleged here are distinguishable from the software copying alleged in Rosciszewski. StateScape argues that the case at bar is distinguishable, because (1) unlike in Rosciszewski, where the case was at summary judgment, discovery has not even begun, and it is not yet known whether all wrongful KSE database accesses constituted copyright infringement, (2) StateScape’s proprietary database, which the defendants allegedly accessed, included both copyrighted and non-copyrighted materials, and (3) the VCCA claim here is “based on elements beyond mere copying, \[including\] false pretenses, embezzlement, and/or conversion.”

As AFSA points out, however, the Complaint consistently alleges that “\[e\]ach of the reports generated by the StateScape proprietary database bears a copyright notice,” that “StateScape owns a copyright in the StateScape proprietary database in the organization of the information in a searchable format available in no other source,” and that “StateScape also owns copyrights in each of the bill summaries within the StateScape database that were original works of authorship.” On those facts as pled by StateScape, it is difficult to see how any claim under the VCCA would contain any elements making it “qualitatively” different from the Copyright Act claims. As such, the VCCA claim is preempted by the Copyright Act and will be dismissed.

Questions

1.What must a plaintiff plead and prove to establish a successful civil claim under the CFAA?

2.Why was the plaintiff’s claim under the Virginia Computer Crimes Act preempted?

3.What is the public policy behind federal preemption?

———

As a postscript to the above case, courts continue to struggle with the meaning of the CFAA terms “without authorization” and “exceeds authorized access” and Congress doesn’t seem to be in any hurry to remedy the confusion. In a case subsequent to the above, WEC Carolina Energy Sols. LLC v. Miller, 687 F.3d 199, 204 (4th Cir. 2012), for instance, the Fourth Circuit Court of Appeals held that the terms ‘without authorization’ and ‘exceeds authorized access’ applies when an individual ‘accesses a computer without permission or obtains or alters information on a computer beyond that which he is authorized to access. See also, Space Systems/Loral, LLC v. Orbital ATK, Inc., 306 F.Supp.3d 845, 852 (E.D.Va. 2102018). Would this standard change the outcome of the above case? There is also a debate about whether password sharing constitutes “unauthorized access” under the CFAA and, if so, under what circumstances. See U.S. v. Nosal, 844 F.3d 1024 (9th Cir. 2016).

The continuing debate around the meaning of these terms cries out for either clarification by the Supreme Court or amendment of the CFAA by Congress, particularly since all of us “assent” to Terms of Use Agreements that arguably restrict our access to certain information. Because the CFAA is both a civil and criminal statute, in effect, Congress has allowed private contracts to define criminal wrongdoing.

Notes

1.The common law misappropriation claim. Although, as noted above, state courts were free after Erie Railroad v. Tompkins to adopt the reasoning of INS and recognize their own cause of action for common law “misappropriation,” (see National Basketball Association v. Motorola, 105 F.3d 841 (2d Cir. 1997) and Mercury Records Productions, Inc. v. Economic Consultants, Inc., 64 Wisc. 2d 163, 218 N.W.2d 705 (1974)), few have done so. As noted in SunPower above, while some states recognize a general claim for “unfair competition” that may apply to information related wrongs, the parameters of these causes of action and how they relate to information that is not protected by trade secret or privacy law are not well-developed. Moreover, such claims are often precluded or preempted by the UTSA or U.S. patent and copyright law. This highlights the value of a holistic approach to information law. Rather than creating a variety of potentially overlapping causes of action to protect information, particularly to prevent the wrongful acquisition of such information, we need to think more critically about the types of information we want our laws to protect and what limits should be placed upon that protection. For suggestions on how this might be done, see Sharon K. Sandeen, Out of Thin Air: Trade Secrets, Cybersecurity, and the Wrongful Acquisition Tort, 19 Minn. J.L. Sci. & Tech. 373 (2018) and Jacqueline Lipton, Information Property: Rights and Responsibilities, 56 Florida. L. Rev. 135 (2004).

2.Idea submission claims. Ideas are a specific type of information and, historically, the alleged misappropriation of ideas has been the basis of both tort and breach of contract claims. See Lionel S. Sobel, The Law of Ideas, Revisited, 1 UCLA Ent. L. Rev. 9 (1994). The typical factual scenario involves an individual who conceives of an idea (often labeled the “idea man”) and then pitches it to a company with the hope that the company will agree to use the idea and compensate him handsomely. As the law governing ideas has evolved, it is clear that the mere sharing of ideas does not create a legal obligation; something else must be shown, usually an express or implied contractual agreement. See e.g., Desny v. Wilder, 46 Cal. 2d. 715 (Cal.1956). Sometimes, however, an implied-at-law duty of confidence may suffice, but this theory of recovery is arguably just a trade secret misappropriation claim under another label. See Robert C. Denicola, The New Law of Ideas, 28 Harv. J.L. & Tech. 211195 (2014); Arthur R. Miller, Common Law Protection for Products of the Mind: An “Idea” Whose Time Has Come, 119 Harv. L. Rev. 703 (2006). Moreover, idea submission claims that do not require proof of an “extra element,” like the existence of a trade secret or a contract, might be preempted by U.S. copyright law.

3.The EU Database Directive. In 1996, the European Union (EU) adopted a sui generis law for the protection of databases. Directive 96/9/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 11 March 1996 on the Legal Protection of Databases, 1996 O.J. (L 77) 20. See also, Mark Schneider, The European Union Database Directive, 13 Berkeley Tech. L.J. 551 (1998). In pertinent part, it requires all members of the EU to adopt laws that grant database owners the right “to prevent extraction and/or re-utilization of the whole or of a substantial part” of a database. Directive 96/9/EC, Article 7(2)(a). Article 1(2) of the EU Database Directive defines a database as a “collection of works, data or other independent materials arranged in a systematic or methodical way and capable of being individually accessed by electronic or other means.”

4.Bibliographic note. In addition to the references above, for more information on the topics discussed in this chapter, see: Shawn E. Tuma, “What Does CFAA Mean and Why Should I Care?” A Primer on the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act for Civil Litigators, 63 S.C. L. Rev. 141, 142 (2011); Neil M. Richards and Daniel J. Solove, Prosser’s Privacy Law: A Mixed Legacy, 98 Calif. L. Rev. 1187 (2010); Sharon K. Sandeen, The Third Party Problem: Assessing the Protection of Information through Tort Law, in Intellectual Property Protection of Fact-Based Works, Copyrights and Its Alternatives (Robert Brauneis, ed., 2009); Vincent R. Johnson, Cybersecurity, Identity Theft, and the Limits of Tort Liability, 57 S.C. L. Rev. 255 (2005); Richard A. Posner, Misappropriation: A Dirge, 40 Hous. L. Rev. 621 (2003); Robert G. Bone, A New Look at Trade Secret Law: Doctrine in Search of Justification, 86 Cal. L. Rev. 241 (1998); Jane C. Ginsburg, Copyright, Common Law, and Sui Generis Protection of Databases in the United States and Abroad, 66 U. Cin. L. Rev. 151 (1997); Wendy J. Gordon, On Owning Information: Intellectual Property and the Restitutionary Impulse, 78 Va. L. Rev. 149 (1992); William L. Prosser, Privacy, 48 Calif. L. Rev. 383 (1960).

Chapter 6

Information Privacy and Data Protection

■ ■ ■

| Anticipated Learning OutcomesAt the conclusion of this chapter, students should be able to: define what is meant by the terms “information privacy” and “data protection”; articulate the basic theories underlying the law; identify the major U.S. laws, rules, and entities that regulate information privacy and data protection; and explain the role of private ordering in information privacy and data protection. |
| --- |

Problem to consider as you read this chapter:

You are a legislative aide for a state legislator. The legislator has asked you to draft a basic privacy statute covering biometric data, like fingerprints and retinal scans. What principles would guide drafting such a law? For instance, how would you define the protected “private information?” Would protection depend upon whether the subject information had been disclosed to others or to the public? Who would be required to protect the information? Could the protections that the law provides be waived by the rightsholder? Should consent to use or disclose the information be obtained from the individuals involved? If so, how? Would the law that you draft limit the permissible uses of the subject information? If not, should the individuals whose biometric data is used receive notice about how the information will be used and whether it will be shared with others? Can you think of other issues that the law should address?

A.Introduction

As you previously learned, information can take many forms and has many definitions. In this chapter we explore what has come to be known as information privacy (also known as data privacy) and data protection. Generally, information privacy concerns the protection of personal, as opposed to business, information, although the collection and use of personal information (often referred to as personally identifiable information or PII) by businesses is at the heart of regulatory concerns regarding privacy. All individuals have the power to keep their personal 214information private, but often it must be shared, for instance, with a doctor. Thus, information privacy laws and regulations usually concern how this shared information can be handled and who has access to it.

Data protection is a broader concept as it concerns the protection of information (data) regardless of whether the information is deemed “private” or “confidential” and often refers to the technical means of securing data. Thus, data protection laws and regulations typically impose obligations on the holders and controllers of data (or information) to secure data from unauthorized access or use.

Information privacy is labeled as such, in part, to distinguish it from the right of privacy that the U.S. Supreme Court has recognized under the U.S. Constitution in cases such as Griswold v. Connecticut, 381 U.S. 479 (1965) (involving the right to marital privacy), Roe v. Wade 410 U.S. 113 (1973) (involving the right to privacy in abortion decisions), and Lawrence v. Texas, 539 US 558 (2003) (involving the right to privacy in sexual relations). However, many of the same privacy concerns that preclude government restrictions on the Constitutional right of privacy are also at the heart of information privacy laws. Additionally, the Supreme Court’s jurisprudence with respect to the Fourth Amendment’s limits on searches and seizure define personal and information privacy in law enforcement situations and influence U.S. conceptions of information privacy more broadly. See e.g., Olmstead v. United States, 277 U.S. 438 (1928); Katz v. United States, 389 U.S. 347 (1967); U.S. v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012); Riley v. California, 573 U.S. 373 (2014); and Carpenter v. United States, 138 S.Ct. 2206 (2018).

It is the job of the information lawyer and information professional to determine which bodies of information must be protected or kept private and how such information can be used, shared, and discarded. Care must be exercised to distinguish legal requirements for information privacy from the legal requirements for data protection, although there is a substantial overlap between the two concepts (which is why they are both discussed in this chapter). One reason for the difference concerns the definitions of “privacy” that are applied in various areas of law. Colloquially, when people think of privacy, they think of personal information that is kept private and not shared with others, but the laws requiring information privacy and data protection are often not so limited. For instance, the four privacy torts that were previously discussed in Chapter 5 do not all involve strictly private or confidential information. Similarly, laws that require data protection often concern information of a defined character, regardless of whether that information has been disclosed to others. For instance, recital 26 of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) states: “The principles of data protection should apply to any information concerning an identified or identifiable natural person.”

215 

Also, it is important to understand that the concept of data protection is not limited to maintaining the privacy, confidentiality, or security of information; it can also concern requirements of data integrity, accuracy, and availability. Thus, there are two key elements of information privacy and data protection law that information lawyers and information professionals should consider: (1) the need of businesses to comply with applicable laws and regulations that, among other requirements, usually require protection for certain defined information; and (2) the privacy and data protection obligations that arise from contractual promises and tort law. (Previously discussed in Chapter 4 and 5, respectively.) Consistent with best information governance practices, it is also important to consider business imperatives, as they might require a company to protect information beyond what applicable law or contracts mandate. Two critical business imperatives are the reputational damage and loss of customers that can result from data breaches and other forms of poor information practices, as Wells Fargo and Facebook have learned in recent years.

Which information privacy and data protection laws apply to a particular business depends upon the nature and scope of a business’ operations and the types of information it collects. If a business only operates within the United States and only collects information from U.S. citizens or residents, then consideration of foreign laws may not be necessary. On the other hand, if a business operates internationally, collects personal information from foreign subjects, or engages in cross-border data transactions, then it must identify all domestic and foreign laws that might apply. This means that multi-national companies need to comply with the information privacy and data protection laws of multiple countries; a situation that may require different policies and procedures for each country or one set of policies and procedures that meet the requirements of all (or most) applicable laws.

Even if a business can limit its focus to U.S. law, information privacy and data protection law in the United States is a mess, or at the very least suffers from a lack of a coherent theory and organization. In part this is due to the different sources of law that comprise U.S. privacy law, which include elements of Constitutional law (state and federal), tort law, contract law, unfair competition law (particularly as enforced by the Federal Trade Commission (FTC)), and federal and state statutes. Fundamentally, this lack of coherence is the result of competing visions on two critical issues: (1) whether and to what extent individuals enjoy, or should enjoy, a right to privacy with respect to information about themselves; and (2) the inability or reluctance of U.S. policymakers to take a comprehensive (omnibus) approach to the regulation of information privacy and data protection.

In the United States, as compared to the European Union (EU), most policymakers tend not to view information privacy as a fundamental right, 216except when it involves a Constitutional right of privacy as defined by the U.S. Supreme Court or state constitutions. Moreover, U.S. jurisprudence surrounding privacy tends to be mired in an examination of one’s use and distribution of personal information, instead of the character of the information itself or the inherent values of personal privacy and data protection. Like the EU’s challenges in the adoption of the GDPR, drafting a comprehensive privacy and data protection law is a similarly monumental challenge for a country as large and diverse as the United States. Every policymaker, company, special interest group, and state seems to have different views on how and what personal information should be protected, and finding consensus is a daunting task.

Another likely reason for the lack of an omnibus approach to regulating information privacy and data protection in the United States concerns the existing and emerging business models that depend upon the collection and use of information of all sorts. In today’s world, numerous companies have developed successful businesses that are highly dependent on their unfettered ability to collect and use personal information. Thus, to impose information privacy and data protection laws and regulations on these businesses would likely require a change to their established business models and they are resistant to that change.

Despite the lack of coherence in U.S. privacy and data protection law, if you ask any person if they have a right to privacy, undoubtedly, they will say that they do, even if they believe that it has been rendered meaningless by technological advances. However, if you ask them to define the parameters of that right, difficulties and differences emerge, particularly if the information in question is shared with others. As Theresa M. Payton and Theodore Claypoole explained in their book, Privacy in the Age of Big Data: Recognizing Threats, Defending Your Rights, and Protecting Your Family (Rowman & Littlefield Pubs. 2014):

We can think of privacy in concentric circles with ourselves in the center. In the middle, held closest to us, are the secrets, thoughts, and rituals that we keep entirely to ourselves and share with no one. Further out are the conversations we have and the actions we take that involve others but that we expect to remain private. We also expect a measure of privacy toward the outer circles, as some issues are kept within the family or inside our company without further publication. Certain information we hide from the neighbors, some financial data we prefer to keep from the government, and there are certain things that our mothers-in-law have no business knowing.

Privacy is complex and personal. Yet no matter what each person’s perception of privacy is, some invasions are so extreme 217that they raise an immediate cry for everyone who hears about them.

This excerpt raises two questions that will animate the rest of this chapter: (1) If we want to regulate privacy and protect the “right to privacy,” where do we draw the line between those invasions that are acceptable and those that are too extreme; and (2) When does the sharing of private information render each of our interests in privacy moot?

The U.S. Supreme Court has repeatedly held that we have a right to privacy under the U.S. Constitution, for example, in cases guaranteeing a woman’s right to an abortion, everyone’s right to marry the person of their choosing and, in conjunction with the Fourth Amendment guarantees against unreasonable searches and seizures. But those protections do not establish a clear and all-encompassing right to privacy. Moreover, they preclude government invasions of privacy, not the sort of invasions by private enterprise that are so prevalent today. Common law tort principles help to fill some of the gaps by recognizing additional privacy interests that the law might protect against invasions by private individuals and entities, as was previously discussed in Lake v. Wal-Mart. Nonetheless, they too stop short of recognizing a broad right to privacy, particularly one that recognizes that certain personal information deserves protection regardless of whether it has been shared with others.

Part of the reason for the limits that are placed on information privacy torts is the reluctance of individuals and businesses to take responsibility for the privacy and information interests of others, usually out of fear of increased liability. But those interests are themselves hard to define. As a result, there is also the vexing question of the nature of the harms suffered in the privacy context, an essential element of our existing privacy torts. Courts and policymakers have difficulty conceptualizing harms that are not direct economic harms, which has led to a tortured application of U.S. privacy law generally. Yet another reason is the influence of Fourth Amendment jurisprudence in limiting privacy rights to what is deemed a “trespass” or a violation of an individual’s “reasonable expectation of privacy” (discussed in Chapter 9), even though what may be deemed reasonable in a law enforcement setting may not be the same as what should be deemed reasonable in other settings, like a doctor’s office. Can you think of other reasons?

Given the complexity of the information privacy and data protection puzzle, and the patchwork nature of U.S. and international privacy laws, it is impossible in this chapter to provide a comprehensive treatment of every privacy and data protection law and regulation. That is the subject of stand-alone textbooks and courses. See e.g., William McGeveran, Privacy and Data Protection Law (West Academic 2016). Rather, the goal of this chapter is to provide an overview of key issues and policy 218choices and to expose you to the principal ways that information privacy and data protection are currently regulated under U.S. law. In keeping with the modalities of regulation that were introduced in Chapter 2, this chapter also discusses the role of private enterprise in defining privacy and data protection expectations and obligations using self-help measures, including private ordering, industry standards, and what has come to be known as “privacy by design.”

The first part of this chapter, Part B, provides background information concerning the right to privacy. It begins with an examination of the parameters of information privacy torts, starting with excerpts from the foundational work on U.S. privacy law, The Right to Privacy, by Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis (the latter a future U.S. Supreme Court Justice). Next, two additional law review articles are excerpted so you can further explore the purpose, meaning, and scope of the right to privacy and why the broader conception of data protection is often needed.

The next two parts of this chapter provide an overview of the principal U.S. federal laws governing information privacy and data protection. It begins in Part C with a discussion of federal privacy statutes of general applicability. In so doing, it explains why all U.S. businesses should adopt privacy and data protection policies and procedures even if they are not subject to a sector-specific law.

Part D of this chapter discusses three federal laws: (1) The Health Information Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA); (2) The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Financial Modernization Act of 1999 (GLB); and (3) the Electronic Communications Privacy Act (ECPA). This will give you a glimpse into: how privacy and data protection statutes are typically structured; what issues are typically addressed; and how the wrongs associated with the collection and use of information might be defined and remedied. Other federal and state laws and regulations that may apply to your client’s business, include: The Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) (15 U.S.C. § 1681 et. seq); the Family Educational Rights & Privacy Act (FERPA) (20 U.S.C. § 1232g); Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (SOX) (Pub. L 107–204); the California Shine the Light Law (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.83–1798.84); the California Consumer Privacy Act (Cal. Civ. Code §§ 1798.100‌–‌1798.199); and the federal Telemarketing Sales Rule (16 CFR 310).

In Part E, the approach of private industry to privacy and data protection concerns is explored through a discussion of privacy contracts and privacy by design. The chapter concludes in Part F with a brief exploration of international law and a summary of the GDPR which, contrary to U.S. law, takes a comprehensive approach to information privacy and data protection that is quickly becoming a model for privacy and data protection regulation worldwide.

219 

As you begin to explore the details of U.S. and international privacy and data protection law, it is important to note that the more comprehensive laws usually address four separate but related issues: (1) information privacy; (2) data protection; (3) information security; and (4) data breach notification. In this book, we address each of these issues in three separate chapters (Chapters 6–8).
