2.Federal Data Breach Notification Laws

The ability to file a lawsuit and obtain compensation or statutory remedies for harm suffered is not the only way that legal obligations are enforced. Particularly where a statute does not create a private right of action, both state and federal laws often place enforcement authority in the chief law enforcement officer (the Attorney General of the United States or of a state) or another administrative agency. For instance, the Attorney General of California is authorized under the Constitution of the State of California and state law (Cal. Govt. Code § 12511) to take charge of “all legal matters in which the State is interested,” which has been interpreted to include the initiation of litigation to enforce applicable law. In recent years, the California Attorney General (as well as the Attorneys General of other states) has brought data breach litigation against such well-known companies as Lenovo Corporation, Target Corporation, and Wells Fargo Bank, as well as lesser known companies. In California, these actions can also be brought by the County District Attorneys on behalf of the People of California. Cal. Govt. Code § 26500.

At the federal level, the enforcement of sector-specific federal laws typically falls on the applicable federal agency. For instance, designated Federal Banking Agencies (including the U.S. Federal Reserve) and the 371Federal Trade Commission (FTC) are responsible for enforcing the information privacy and data security provisions of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (GLB) and the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, Office of Civil Rights (OCR) is responsible for enforcing the privacy and data security provisions of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA). In addition, based upon its statutory mandate, as previously discussed in Chapters 6 and 7, the FTC plays an active role in overseeing the information practices of companies, including with respect to data breach notification requirements.

Despite the absence of a comprehensive U.S. federal law similar to the GDPR, the FTC has long exercised oversight of information practices under the Federal Trade Commission Act, Section 5, which, in pertinent part, empowers the FTC to prevent individuals and businesses (except banks and other types of businesses that are regulated elsewhere) “from using unfair methods of competition in or affecting commerce and unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.” 15 U.S.C. § 45(a). The FTC is also the designated agency for the enforcement of: The Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (15 U.S.C. § 6501–6506); The Fair Credit Reporting Act (15 U.S.C. § 1681–1681x); The Health Information Technology (HITECH) Provisions of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009 (Pub. L. No. 111-5, 123 Stat. 115, codified in relevant part at 42 U.S.C. § 17937 and 17953); The Identity Theft Assumption and Deterrence Act of 1998 (Pub. L. 105-318, 112 Stat. 3010, codified in relevant part at 18 U.S.C. § 1028); and other federal laws.

Although federal legislation titled “The Personal Data Protection and Notification Act” was first introduced in Congress in 2015 and has been subsequently reintroduced, federal law governing data breach notification is not yet comprehensive or uniform. The principal U.S. federal data breach notification requirements are: (1) the FTC’s Health Breach Notification Rule (for companies not subject to HIPAA as required pursuant to the HITECH Act) (16 CFR Part 318) (discussed below); (2) the HIPAA Breach Notification Rule (45 CFR 164.400–414); and (3) the Interagency Guidelines Establishing Information Security Standards (12 CFR 364, Appendix B) (for companies subject to GLB).

Because of the regulatory complexity, the FTC generally recommends that companies that suffer a data breach first notify law enforcement of the breach and then take steps to notify affected individuals and businesses, in accordance with both state law and federal rules and standards as applicable. As part of its educational mission and to improve and streamline the data breach notification process, the FTC issued Data Breach Response: A Guide for Business in 2016 which includes a sample Notification Letter.

372 

As a sample of federal requirements, the following is the FTC’s data breach notification rules for healthcare providers. As you read these rules, consider the core questions that were asked above with respect to California’s data breach notification requirements.

FTC Health Breach Notification Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 318

§ 318.1Purpose and scope.

(a)This part, which shall be called the “Health Breach Notification Rule,” implements section 13407 of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009. It applies to foreign and domestic vendors of personal health records, PHR related entities, and third party service providers, irrespective of any jurisdictional tests in the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Act, that maintain information of U.S. citizens or residents. It does not apply to HIPAA-covered entities, or to any other entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity.

(b)This part preempts state law as set forth in section 13421 of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009.

§ 318.2Definitions.

(a)Breach of security means, with respect to unsecured PHR identifiable health information of an individual in a personal health record, acquisition of such information without the authorization of the individual. Unauthorized acquisition will be presumed to include unauthorized access to unsecured PHR identifiable health information unless the vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider that experienced the breach has reliable evidence showing that there has not been, or could not reasonably have been, unauthorized acquisition of such information.

(b)Business associate means a business associate under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, Public Law 104-191, 110 Stat. 1936, as defined in 45 CFR 160.103.

(c)HIPAA\-covered entity means a covered entity under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act, Public Law 104-191, 110 Stat. 1936, as defined in 45 CFR 160.103.

(d)Personal health record means an electronic record of PHR identifiable health information on an individual that can be drawn from multiple sources and that is managed, shared, and controlled by or primarily for the individual.

(e)PHR identifiable health information means “individually identifiable health information,” as defined in section 1171(6) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1320d(6)), and, with respect to an individual, information:

(1)That is provided by or on behalf of the individual; and

373 

(2)That identifies the individual or with respect to which there is a reasonable basis to believe that the information can be used to identify the individual.

(f)PHR related entity means an entity, other than a HIPAA-covered entity or an entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity, that:

(1)Offers products or services through the Web site of a vendor of personal health records;

(2)Offers products or services through the Web sites of HIPAA-covered entities that offer individuals personal health records; or

(3)Accesses information in a personal health record or sends information to a personal health record.

(g)State means any of the several States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the Virgin Islands, Guam, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands.

(h)Third party service provider means an entity that:

(1)Provides services to a vendor of personal health records in connection with the offering or maintenance of a personal health record or to a PHR related entity in connection with a product or service offered by that entity; and

(2)Accesses, maintains, retains, modifies, records, stores, destroys, or otherwise holds, uses, or discloses unsecured PHR identifiable health information as a result of such services.

(i)Unsecured means PHR identifiable information that is not protected through the use of a technology or methodology specified by the Secretary of Health and Human Services in the guidance issued under section 13402(h)(2) of the American Reinvestment and Recovery Act of 2009.

(j)Vendor of personal health records means an entity, other than a HIPAA-covered entity or an entity to the extent that it engages in activities as a business associate of a HIPAA-covered entity, that offers or maintains a personal health record.

§ 318.3Breach notification requirement.

(a)In general. In accordance with §§ 318.4, 318.5, and 318.6, each vendor of personal health records, following the discovery of a breach of security of unsecured PHR identifiable health information that is in a personal health record maintained or offered by such vendor, and each PHR related entity, following the discovery of a breach of security of such information that is obtained through a product or service provided by such entity, shall:

374 

(1)Notify each individual who is a citizen or resident of the United States whose unsecured PHR identifiable health information was acquired by an unauthorized person as a result of such breach of security; and

(2)Notify the Federal Trade Commission.

(b)Third party service providers. A third party service provider shall, following the discovery of a breach of security, provide notice of the breach to an official designated in a written contract by the vendor of personal health records or the PHR related entity to receive such notices or, if such a designation is not made, to a senior official at the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity to which it provides services, and obtain acknowledgment from such official that such notice was received. Such notification shall include the identification of each customer of the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity whose unsecured PHR identifiable health information has been, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired during such breach. For purposes of ensuring implementation of this requirement, vendors of personal health records and PHR related entities shall notify third party service providers of their status as vendors of personal health records or PHR related entities subject to this Part.

(c)Breaches treated as discovered. A breach of security shall be treated as discovered as of the first day on which such breach is known or reasonably should have been known to the vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider, respectively. Such vendor, entity, or third party service provider shall be deemed to have knowledge of a breach if such breach is known, or reasonably should have been known, to any person, other than the person committing the breach, who is an employee, officer, or other agent of such vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, or third party service provider.

§ 318.4Timeliness of notification.

(a)In general. Except as provided in paragraph (c) of this section and § 318.5(c), all notifications required under §§ 318.3(a)(1), 318.3(b), and 318.5(b) shall be sent without unreasonable delay and in no case later than 60 calendar days after the discovery of a breach of security.

(b)Burden of proof. The vendor of personal health records, PHR related entity, and third party service provider involved shall have the burden of demonstrating that all notifications were made as required under this Part, including evidence demonstrating the necessity of any delay.

(c)Law enforcement exception. If a law enforcement official determines that a notification, notice, or posting required under this Part would impede a criminal investigation or cause damage to national security, such notification, notice, or posting shall be delayed. This paragraph shall be 375implemented in the same manner as provided under 45 CFR 164.528(a)(2), in the case of a disclosure covered under such section.

§ 318.5Methods of notice.

(a)Individual notice. A vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity that discovers a breach of security shall provide notice of such breach to an individual promptly, as described in § 318.4, and in the following form:

(1)Written notice, by first-class mail to the individual at the last known address of the individual, or by email, if the individual is given a clear, conspicuous, and reasonable opportunity to receive notification by first-class mail, and the individual does not exercise that choice. If the individual is deceased, the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity that discovered the breach must provide such notice to the next of kin of the individual if the individual had provided contact information for his or her next of kin, along with authorization to contact them. The notice may be provided in one or more mailings as information is available.

(2)If, after making reasonable efforts to contact all individuals to whom notice is required under § 318.3(a), through the means provided in paragraph (a)(1) of this section, the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity finds that contact information for ten or more individuals is insufficient or out-of-date, the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity shall provide substitute notice, which shall be reasonably calculated to reach the individuals affected by the breach, in the following form:

(i)Through a conspicuous posting for a period of 90 days on the home page of its Web site; or

(ii)In major print or broadcast media, including major media in geographic areas where the individuals affected by the breach likely reside. Such a notice in media or web posting shall include a toll-free phone number, which shall remain active for at least 90 days, where an individual can learn whether or not the individual’s unsecured PHR identifiable health information may be included in the breach.

(3)In any case deemed by the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity to require urgency because of possible imminent misuse of unsecured PHR identifiable health information, that entity may provide information to individuals by telephone or other means, as appropriate, in addition to notice provided under paragraph (a)(1) of this section.

(b)Notice to media. A vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity shall provide notice to prominent media outlets serving a State or jurisdiction, following the discovery of a breach of security, if the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more residents of such State 376or jurisdiction is, or is reasonably believed to have been, acquired during such breach.

(c)Notice to FTC. Vendors of personal health records and PHR related entities shall provide notice to the Federal Trade Commission following the discovery of a breach of security. If the breach involves the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of 500 or more individuals, then such notice shall be provided as soon as possible and in no case later than ten business days following the date of discovery of the breach. If the breach involves the unsecured PHR identifiable health information of fewer than 500 individuals, the vendor of personal health records or PHR related entity may maintain a log of any such breach, and submit such a log annually to the Federal Trade Commission no later than 60 calendar days following the end of the calendar year, documenting breaches from the preceding calendar year. All notices pursuant to this paragraph shall be provided according to instructions at the Federal Trade Commission’s Web site.

§ 318.6Content of notice.

Regardless of the method by which notice is provided to individuals under § 318.5 of this part, notice of a breach of security shall be in plain language and include, to the extent possible, the following:

(a)A brief description of what happened, including the date of the breach and the date of the discovery of the breach, if known;

(b)A description of the types of unsecured PHR identifiable health information that were involved in the breach (such as full name, Social Security number, date of birth, home address, account number, or disability code);

(c)Steps individuals should take to protect themselves from potential harm resulting from the breach;

(d)A brief description of what the entity that suffered the breach is doing to investigate the breach, to mitigate harm, and to protect against any further breaches; and

(e)Contact procedures for individuals to ask questions or learn additional information, which shall include a toll-free telephone number, an email address, Web site, or postal address.

§ 318.7Enforcement.

A violation of this part shall be treated as an unfair or deceptive act or practice in violation of a regulation under § 18(a)(1)(B) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(a)(1)(B)) regarding unfair or deceptive acts or practices.

The foregoing are examples of the numerous federal and state data breach notification laws that exist in the United States. Unfortunately, while similar in the topics they cover, the details of these laws can vary, particularly with respect to when, how, and to whom a notice of a data breach must be given. Recall also that the Securities and Exchange Commission’s (SEC) reporting and notice requirements may apply to data breaches, adding another level of complexity that makes compliance difficult. See discussion of SEC oversight in Chapters 6 and 12. Moreover, the GDPR contains data breach notification requirements that may apply, including a very short deadline (72 hours) in which notification must be given. See Notes below.

D.Practical, Non-Legal Approaches to Data Breaches

As you’ve read, data breaches require quick and thoughtful action, and much of a company’s information security efforts should focus on preventing, detecting, and minimizing data breaches. The reasons are many. Beyond the potential harm to consumers, data breaches often result in reputational harms that can diminish customer goodwill, company profits, and stock valuation. They are also likely to engender increased 378scrutiny by shareholders, politicians, and government regulators. (As Facebook found out in early 2018 when it was revealed that Cambridge Analytica was given access to customer information that Facebook collected.) Data breaches can also result in the loss of valuable trade secrets and other confidential and proprietary information of a business and the disclosure of embarrassing private facts. For instance, the 2014 breach of information held by Sony Pictures revealed embarrassing emails about Hollywood celebrities, including information about gender pay inequity.

As this chapter explains, at a minimum, businesses that collect personal information from customers should comply with all applicable laws concerning the collection, handling, use, and disposal of such information, including applicable data breach notification requirements. But throughout information law practice there are also practical actions that should be considered but are not necessarily required by law. Data breach response is no exception.

One practical action is to organize an incident response team and develop a response plan to be implemented in the event of a security incident or data breach. Although companies should primarily engage in efforts which are designed to prevent data breaches, they should also assume a data breach will occur and plan and train accordingly. Attorneys and information professionals can greatly assist clients to prepare and implement such a plan; one that addresses both the short-term and long-term needs of a client.

Of course, before a company can respond to a data breach it must be made aware of the breach. Companies should not wait for problems to be reported when best practices (including the National Security Agency’s 20 Critical Security Controls discussed in Chapter 7) require the institution of protocols and processes that are designed to pinpoint vulnerabilities and quickly identify security incidents and data breaches. This includes active monitoring of data and computer system usage that looks for unusual behaviors, unauthorized access, and spikes in data flows. Generally, this is a job for computer scientists and IT specialists, and numerous companies and services exist to provide monitoring services, but attorneys and information professionals can and should review and understand the scope of a client’s monitoring efforts and look for any gaps and vulnerabilities.

The FTC’s Data Breach Response: A Guide for Business, lists various steps that should be taken (and planned for) once a data breach is identified. Obviously, steps should be taken immediately to plug any gaps in data security and preserve evidence of wrongdoing. Also, consideration should be given to notifying law enforcement about the breach. To enhance the ability of law enforcement to investigate and gather evidence, it may be appropriate to delay notifying affected parties of the breach (assuming this can be done without violating applicable data breach notification laws), 379but a plan for such notification should be developed and implemented when appropriate and as required by law. The FTC Guide also recommends:

Have a communications plan. Create a comprehensive plan that reaches all affected audiences—employees, customers, investors, business partners, and other stakeholders. Don’t make misleading statements about the breach. And don’t withhold key details that might help consumers protect themselves and their information. Also, don’t publicly share information that might put consumers at further risk. Anticipate questions that people will ask. Then, put top tier questions and clear, plain-language answers on your website where they are easy to find. Good communication up front can limit customers’ concerns and frustration, saving your company time and money later.

Another important aspect of a company’s response to a data breach is to determine what went wrong and use the experience of the breach to improve its information security plans, policies, and processes going forward.

Of course, once news of a data breach is released to the public, it is probable that a class action lawsuit will follow, but actual and potential harm to consumers can be minimized with appropriate action, thereby increasing the likelihood that any resulting litigation will be dismissed for lack of cognizable harm. For instance, companies have been known to offer free credit monitoring services to reduce actual losses to consumers and alleviate any fear of future data breach related harms.

| What Do You Think?Given its importance to consumers and others, should the law require that companies have a published and publicly-available data breach response plan? After all, the law requires such behavior in other contexts. See e.g., 17 U.S.C. § 512 (copyright law’s “notice and takedown” procedure for online copyright infringement, which identifies a number of things that an entity must do to avail itself of the “safe harbor” of the DMCA.) If so, why? If not, what’s the concern? Regardless of your answer, what seem to be the most important elements of a response, and why? |

Notes

1.The California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018. When it goes into effect on January 1, 2020 (and unless amended or preempted by federal law), the California Consumer Privacy Act of 2018 (CCPA) (adding Title 1.81.5 (commencing with Section 1798.100) to Part 4 of Division 3 of the Civil Code), should have a significant impact on data breach litigation in California because of its comprehensive approach to data privacy and protection (see discussion 380in Chapter 6). Among the most significant provisions is California Civil Code § 1798.150(a) which is designed to get around the Spokeo problem (discussed above and in Chapter 6) by specifying statutory damages in the event of a data breach. In pertinent part, it provides that:

(1) Any consumer whose nonencrypted or nonredacted personal information, as defined in subparagraph (A) of paragraph (1) of subdivision (d) of Section 1798.81.5, is subject to an unauthorized access and exfiltration, theft, or disclosure as a result of the business’ violation of the duty to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of the information to protect the personal information may institute a civil action for any of the following:

(A)To recover damages in an amount not less than one hundred dollars ($100) and not greater than seven hundred and fifty ($750) per consumer per incident or actual damages, whichever is greater.

(B)Injunctive or declaratory relief.

(C)Any other relief the court deems proper

Other provisions of the CCPA give consumers various rights with respect to the collection and use of their personal information. As of this writing, the California legislature is actively considering a number of amendments to the CCPA. Information lawyers will need to pay close attention to developments regarding this groundbreaking and potentially far-reaching law.

2.Data disposal laws. In addition to adopting data breach notification laws, more than half of the states have adopted data disposal laws and the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has issued its Disposal Rule. This is in addition to other laws and regulations that impose data retention and disposal requirements. According to the FTC website:

The Disposal Rule applies to consumer reports or information derived from consumer reports. The Fair Credit Reporting Act defines the term consumer report to include information obtained from a consumer reporting company that is used—or expected to be used—in establishing a consumer’s eligibility for credit, employment, or insurance, among other purposes. Credit reports and credit scores are consumer reports. So are reports businesses or individuals receive with information relating to employment background, check writing history, insurance claims, residential or tenant history, or medical history.

The Disposal Rule requires disposal practices that are reasonable and appropriate to prevent the unauthorized access to—or use of—information in a consumer report. For example, reasonable measures for disposing of consumer report information could include establishing and complying with policies to:

381 

*   burn, pulverize, or shred papers containing consumer report information so that the information cannot be read or reconstructed;

*   destroy or erase electronic files or media containing consumer report information so that the information cannot be read or reconstructed;

*   conduct due diligence and hire a document destruction contractor to dispose of material specifically identified as consumer report information consistent with the Rule. Due diligence could include:

*   reviewing an independent audit of a disposal company’s operations and/or its compliance with the Rule;

*   obtaining information about the disposal company from several references;

*   requiring that the disposal company be certified by a recognized trade association;

*   reviewing and evaluating the disposal company’s information security policies or procedures.

State laws have been enacted which impose similar requirements, but with respect to a potentially broader set of information. For instance, California Civil Code § 1798.81, provides:

A business shall take all reasonable steps to dispose, or arrange for the disposal, of customer records within its custody or control containing personal information when the records are no longer to be retained by the business by (a) shredding, (b) erasing, or (c) otherwise modifying the personal information in those records to make it unreadable or undecipherable through any means.

Company policies concerning the disposal of information must also comply with laws, regulations, and best practices that often require information to be retained and stored for specific periods of time. See e.g., Cal. Civil Code § 1785.14(b). This topic is discussed in Part III with respect to litigation hold rules and securities regulations governing the maintenance of corporate records and tax filings.

3.The GDPR’s data breach notification requirements. Articles 33 and 34 of the GDPR sets forth the governing law for data breach notifications. In pertinent part, Article 33 provides that:

In the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after having become aware of it, notify the personal data breach to the supervisory authority competent in accordance with Article 55, unless the personal data breach is unlikely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons. Where the notification to the 382supervisory authority is not made within 72 hours, it shall be accompanied by reasons for the delay.

Article 34 is the provision requiring notice to the data subject. Subsection 1 states:

When the personal data breach is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall communicate the personal data breach to the data subject without undue delay.

The required notification must, at a minimum: (1) describe the nature of the personal data breach including where possible, the categories and approximate number of data subjects concerned and the categories and approximate number of personal data records concerned; (2) communicate the name and contact details of the data protection officer or other contact point where more information can be obtained; (3) describe the likely consequences of the personal data breach; and (4) describe the measures taken or proposed to be taken by the controller to address the personal data breach, including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects.

Prop. 45, 46 (2015); Ryan Calo, Privacy Harm Exceptionalism, 12 J. Telecomm. & High Tech. L. 361, 361, 364 (2014); Rachael M. Peters, So You’ve Been Notified, Now What? Chapter 9

Information Crimes

■ ■ ■

| Anticipated Learning OutcomesAt the conclusion of this chapter, students should be able to: articulate the principal differences between civil and criminal liability related to the misappropriation of information; identify the major criminal statutes that make information related wrongs a crime; and articulate the bad acts (actus reus) and state of mind (mens rea) that are considered criminal. |

Problem to consider as you read this chapter:

Jana Smith is excited. She recently graduated from college and got her first “real” job working for a high-tech company in Silicon Valley as a software programmer. The application and interviewing process was grueling as it included a psychological profile, a drug test, a review of her social media postings, and a credit check.

On her first day of work, Ms. Smith met with representatives of her company’s Human Resources Department and was required to sign a series of documents, none of which she was given time to read ahead of time, including: (1) a non-disclosure agreement (NDA); (2) an invention assignment agreement; and (3) an employment agreement. Both the NDA and employment agreement included provisions concerning the use of the Company’s computer systems, including: restrictions on accessing company computers remotely on a non-company issued computer; limits on the use of removable storage devices (e.g., USB, SD cards, and flash drives), and the company’s password and encryption policies. Would you advise her to sign these documents? What provisions and terms would you advise Jana to read closely?

A.Introduction

If you think that information is property, then it does not take a great leap of logic to assume that the “wrongful acquisition” or “theft” of information should be punished criminally. Even before the advent of personal computers and the internet, the behavior of those who obtained information from others under nefarious circumstances was often deemed an act of unfair competition as Dupont v. Christopher in Chapter 1 reveals. 384Some state legislatures adopted criminal statutes that could extend to such acts, provided the specified criminal actus reus and mens rea could be proven. Generally, however, information theft (and, in fact, intellectual property theft) was not of great concern to legislators of earlier times, in part, because information did not exist in the forms or orders of magnitude that it does now and because of the definitional problems that were discussed in Chapter 1.

At common law, except for unpublished writings, trade secrets, and some common law theories for the protection of other types of confidential information, intangible information was not typically viewed as being a valuable, privately-held asset. Moreover, the common law causes of action that had developed to provide civil claims for relief were generally deemed sufficient to regulate bad behaviors vis-à-vis information. (Recall the discussion of those common law claims in Chapter 5.)

| What Do You Think?Consider why criminal penalties for the wrongful taking of information are sparse? What difficulties might a legislator encounter when trying to fashion a criminal law to regulate the acquisition, disclosure, or use of information? What are the countervailing public policy interests at play? Does it depend on which definition of information (from Chapter 1) is used? |
| --- |

In her article, The Puzzle of Criminal Sanctions for IP Infringement, 24 Harv. J.L. & Tech 469, 474–475 (2011), Professor Irina Manta examined why aspects of both trademark and copyright (but not patent) infringement became crimes under U.S. law, raising questions that are also applicable to information related behaviors more generally. She explained:

One scholar \[Gretchen Moohr\] explains that criminal law and IP began intersecting “largely because of increases in the value of intangible property and growth in its variations.” Then, as policymakers began applying criminal law to IP offenses, the intangible material in question became increasingly “propertize\[d\]” and the discussion mostly shifted from whether IP infringement should be criminalized at all to which particular instances of infringement merit criminal punishment. This may have dovetailed with the larger trend in the criminalization of theft given that there has been a

long history of expansion of the role of the criminal law in protecting property. That history begins with a concern for crimes of violence—in the present context, the taking of property by force from the possession of another, i.e., robbery. The criminal law then expanded, by means of the ancient quasi-criminal writ of trespass, to cover all taking of another’s 385property from his possession without his consent, even though no force was used. This misconduct was punished as larceny. \[Citing the Model Penal Code § 223.1 cmt. 2(a) (1980).\]

When it comes to IP, the law went a step further. Not only is force rarely involved in IP infringement, but the law must grapple with the question of what exactly is taken or stolen. Indeed, because IP tends to be both intangible and non-rivalrous, its infringement causes at most a reduction in value as opposed to a genuine “taking” of the good. Perhaps in the criminal context such infringement would often be more akin to other property crimes than it is to theft.

The same questions can be applied to information more generally. Specifically: (1) is the information property?; (2) is the concern an act of violence, for instance the means of acquiring the information?; and, if not (3) do we want to recognize a trespassory wrong? More broadly, as Professor Manta explained: “much of the moral and utilitarian reasons for criminal sanctions revolve around (1) the harm done to IP owners and (2) the ability of criminal laws to prevent these harms.”

When you think about the crimes that are typically taught in a criminal law course, they fall into two general categories: crimes against people (like battery and homicide) and crimes against property (like theft). Since information is not a person, unless information (or a particular type of information) is classified as property or quasi-property for criminal law purposes, information related wrongs do not fit easily into traditional notions of criminal wrongdoing. Thus, the greatest impediment to imposing criminal liability has been convincing courts that the allegedly purloined information is property for purposes of existing criminal property statutes, or that the criminal property statutes were intended to cover intangible as well as tangible property. Since information is not property unless the law says it is property, any criminal statute that seeks to punish the “theft” of information, must first define the metes and bounds of that property interest.

In the absence of a property interest, information related bad acts could be made the subject of criminal sanctions through legislation designed to address specified wrongdoing, but then difficulties arise in defining the wrongdoing without relationship to a property interest. In his article, Crimes Involving Intangible Property, 11 U.N.H. L. Rev. 171 (2013), Professor Thomas G. Field, surveyed the federal and state criminal laws for the protection of intangible property and could not find many. At the federal level, he identified only the Economic Espionage Act of 1996 (EEA) and the criminal provisions of the Copyright Act (both discussed below). At the state level, he concluded that roughly half of the states have adopted 386criminal trade secret theft statutes, but problematically, with varying definitions of trade secrets which often conflict with the definition of a trade secret under civil law (the criminal law of Texas is the subject of Schalk v. State of Texas, reprinted below).

Moreover, as Professor Field pointed out, state criminal laws that prohibit the copying of information might be preempted by the U.S. Copyright Act. Professor Field also explained that some states adopted statutes, likely based upon the Model Penal Code, to penalize the theft of “intangible personal property” but without defining what that term means. Alas, laws can have ill-defined or undefined terms, although legislators usually attempt to avoid such problems. As a result, the criminal law with respect to information is, at best, underdeveloped and, at worst, spotty and inconsistent.

Gaps in criminal laws related to information wrongs, particularly the misappropriation of trade secrets, led Congress to pass the Economic Espionage Act of 1996 (EEA), but for a variety of reasons this effort has not resulted in a lot of criminal prosecutions. One reason is because of the reluctance of trade secret owners to report trade secret theft to law enforcement authorities for fear that they will lose control of their trade secrets and because the pendency of a criminal case is likely to result in a stay of the associated civil case. Law enforcement is also reluctant to take on these cases because of the difficulty and expense of obtaining convictions and because trade secret owners have a robust civil remedy. See Michelle Evans, Effectiveness of Available Civil Remedies As A Factor Influencing Prosecution of Economic Espionage Act Cases, 57 Washburn L.J. 463 (2018). Of course, as is often the case, a lack of law enforcement resources may also play a role in the relative paucity of EEA prosecutions.

A related, and arguably more successful, approach has been the adoption of criminal statutes which are not necessarily dependent upon the existence of an identifiable property interest but instead target the sorts of bad behaviors that computers and the digitization of information make possible. These are often referred to as “computer crimes.” In the introduction to his casebook, Computer Crime Law (West Academic 2018), Professor Orin Kerr explains:

There are two reasons to label criminal conduct a computer crime. First, an individual might use a computer to engage in criminal activity. Second, the evidence needed to prove a crime might be stored in computerized form. The law governing the use of a computer to commit a crime is substantive computer crime law, because it concerns the scope of substantive conduct that has been criminalized. The law governing the collection of computerized evidence is procedural computer crime law, because it concerns 387the legal procedures investigators can use to collect digital evidence in criminal investigations.

Both types of computer crime laws can relate to the acquisition, disclosure, or use of information, but not all of them do.

This chapter focuses on substantive computer crime laws and other criminal statutes that prohibit the wrongful access to or wrongful acquisition, disclosure, or use of information (whether stored in a computer or not). A course focused on Fourth Amendment jurisprudence or that uses Professor Kerr’s book would teach procedural computer crime laws related to both information stored in a computer (also known as “information at rest”) and information transmitted via a communications network (“also known as “information in transit”). For a preview, see the Notes at the end of this chapter.

Our discussion of substantive computer crime law begins with an exploration of stolen property statutes and some of the difficulties of applying those statutes to information alleged to have been stolen. It then shifts its focus to a discussion of trade secret theft statutes. Lastly, the criminal provisions of the Copyright Act and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) are discussed. (Recall that you learned about the civil claims under both statutes in Chapter 5.) As you will see, some information related criminal laws focus on specified types of information, while others focus on specified wrongful behaviors. But regardless of focus, they all include mens rea (state of mind) and actus reus (bad act) requirements that must be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. These requirements serve to distinguish information crimes from information torts, but to what extent is often the question.

As you read the materials that follow, keep in mind that there may be additional state and federal criminal statutes that apply to information theft and other information related behaviors. For instance, before computer crime specific statutes were adopted by Congress and state legislators, federal and state prosecutors relied upon various non-computer specific laws. See Peter J.G. Toren, The Prosecution of Trade Secrets Thefts Under Federal Law, 22 Pepp. L. Rev. 59 (1994) (discussing federal trade secret prosecutions before the enactment of the EEA). In 1984, a report issued by the American Bar Association (ABA) Task Force on Computer Crime, Section of Criminal Justice, titled Report on Computer Crime, identified laws governing wire fraud, trespass, and embezzlement as potential computer crimes.

| 388 What Do You Think?As you read the cases that follow, pay close attention to the essential elements of the crimes and consider how they differ from the elements of the tort claims that were discussed in Chapter 5. How does the state of mind (mens rea) requirement differ from applicable civil counterparts? How does the bad act (actus reus) requirement differ? Can you articulate why criminal laws are more specific than tort claims? |
