C.Legal and Contractual Obligations of Confidentiality

As explained in the foregoing commentary to Minnesota Rules of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.6, lawyers and law firms are often under legal or contractual obligations to maintain the confidentiality of information that exist separate and apart from applicable rules of professional conduct. These obligations may be imposed directly by clients or applicable law, or indirectly due to the nature of the documents being handled on behalf of a client. They may also be imposed by third parties or by court order, for instance, when parties involved in litigation agree to a confidentiality agreement or a court issues a protective order.

698 

While it is impossible to detail all the laws and regulations that may impose legal obligations on lawyers and law firms to maintain the confidentiality and security of information, a general observation can be offered: usually, legal obligations concerning information are triggered either: (1) by the nature of the information (if it is confidential or sensitive); or (2) the status of the person or entity handling the information. For instance, as previously discussed in Chapter 15, a lawyer may have an obligation to maintain the confidentiality of information that is deemed to be a matter of national security. Similarly, due to the loss of trade secret and patent rights that can result from the disclosure of information about a client’s invention, lawyers who handle such information have an obligation to determine the client’s intentions as to the information’s use, and if a patent is contemplated, ensure that it is kept confidential until any resulting patent application is published. Also, it has long been recognized that various trustees and fiduciaries have duties of confidentiality with respect to certain information.

Generally, if a client owes duties of confidentiality and security with respect to certain information, then the lawyers and law firms who represent those clients should assume that those duties apply to them as well. Thus, the best practice is for lawyers and law firms to treat all information received from a client or third party as confidential until it is determined that it need not be so protected. However, some laws may impose additional obligations (such as required disclosures, agreements, and security measures), so merely keeping information that is received from a client confidential may not suffice to meet applicable obligations. For instance, due to their own privacy and cybersecurity obligations, an increasing number of businesses are insisting that their attorneys meet prescribed information security standards.

When legal obligations of confidentiality and security are tied to the nature of the information, rather than to the identity of the person handling the information, it can be difficult to identify who has the duty of confidence. Moreover, even when laws impose confidentiality obligations on specific types of individuals or entities, it may not be immediately obvious that those individuals and entities include lawyers and law firms. The Health Information Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), discussed in Chapter 6, provide two examples. Under HIPAA, lawyers who handle personal health information (PHI) will be subject to the dictates of the HIPAA Privacy Rule and Security Rule (see 45 C.F.R. Parts 160 and 164) if they are considered “business associates” as defined (45 C.F.R. § 160.103). Similarly, the GDPR applies broadly to:

\[T\]he processing of personal data of data subjects who are in the Union by a controller or processor not established in the Union, where the processing activities are related to (a) the offering of 699goods or services, . . .; or (b) the monitoring of their behavior as far as their behavior takes place with the Union.

GDPR, Article 3(2). Thus, a United States law firm that offers or provides services to an EU citizen is obligated to comply with the GDPR. Lawyers and law firms that are victimized by computer hackers may also be subject to data breach notification laws, depending upon the nature of the information that is hacked. See Chapter 8 and the laws cited therein.

With respect to a lawyer’s or law firm’s contractual obligations of confidentiality, they can arise in several different situations. First, a client may insist on a confidentiality or nondisclosure agreement (NDA) to supplement a lawyer’s and law firm’s professional duty of confidentiality. In fact, various laws require contracts of this sort, for instance the “Business Associate Agreements” that are required under HIPAA. See 45 CFR § 164.504(e).

Second, a contractual obligation of confidentiality or security may arise in conjunction with a business deal that a lawyer or law firm is negotiating on behalf of a client. Typically, these agreements explicitly bind the lawyers and law firms representing the parties or, at the very least, apply to the parties’ agents, which would include the involved attorneys.

Third, lawyers and law firms that handle litigation are usually bound by associated confidentiality agreements and protective orders. Often, these agreements can be quite detailed in specifying who has access to the subject information and how it should be handled and shared.

Lastly, lawyers and law firms may be bound to duties of confidentiality in conjunction with their business dealings with vendors. For instance, they may be contractually obligated to maintain the confidentiality and secrecy of the computer software and applications they use.

Once a lawyer’s and law firm’s duties of confidentiality and security are determined, steps must be taken to ensure that appropriate information governance processes and methods are implemented. There is a growing market for information security services directed at law firms, including training modules. These efforts are aimed at creating a culture that takes information security seriously and is usually a work-in-progress. To create such a culture, lawyers and law firms should install a process for determining the legal obligations that attach to all the information they create, use, and handle; in other words, an IG plan. See Chapter 11.

The privacy and security frameworks that were discussed in previous chapters, and that continue to be developed by government and non-government entities, also provide useful recommendations and guidance to lawyers and law firms. As above, you should consider the practical limitations associated with creating such a robust information security program at a firm.

700 

D.Ownership of Client Files and Work Product

An issue that sometimes arises in law practice concerns the ownership of information and documents, particularly with respect to so-called “client files;” that is, the collection of information and documents that lawyers and law firms typically create in the course of representing a client. The general rule (backed-up by ABA Model Rule of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.16(d)) is that the client is entitled, upon request, to the return or transfer of “its” information. However, jurisdictions differ with respect to the precise identity of the information that a client owns and, depending upon the nature of the information, the issue of ownership may be more of a question of law than legal ethics. See Allison D. Rhodes & Robert W. Hillman, Client Files and Digital Law Practices: Rethinking Old Concepts in an Era of Lawyer Mobility, 43 Suffolk U. L. Rev. 897, 901 (2010) (noting: “Although the primacy of clients’ rights in their files is largely accepted, the task of defining what constitutes the “file” in which the client has rights remains problematic.”)

Some states recognize that the client owns the entire file, including the work-product of its attorneys, while other states deem work-product to belong to the attorney(s) who created it. See, e.g., Mass. R. Prof. C. 1.15A (stating that client owns entire file, including work product); Ark. R. Prof. C. 1.19 (stating that “client files” do not include the attorneys’ work product). Other states have held that the client file is owned by the client’s lawyers, except for any documents provided by the client. See, e.g., Brown v. State, 93 So. 3d 1194, 1196 (Fla. Dist. Ct. App. 2012) (stating that generally client files are the “attorney’s personal property.”) (Citation and internal quotation marks omitted). Thus, lawyers and law firms must become familiar with the applicable law of the jurisdictions in which they practice so that they can abide by it when implementing their IG plan.

The following case provides an example of the scope and nature of information ownership and access disputes between law firms and their former clients. Often, they either concern a dispute regarding a client’s entitlement to the attorney’s work product or the ability of an attorney or law firm to impose a lien on client files until outstanding legal fees are paid.

Sage Realty Corp. v. Proskauer Rose Goetz & Mendelsohn L.L.P.

Court of Appeals of New York, 1997  
[91 N.Y.2d 30](http://lawschool.westlaw.com/shared/westlawRedirect.aspx?task=find&cite=91+N.Y.2d+30&appflag=67.12)

Levine, Judge.

In 1994, petitioners retained Proskauer Rose Goetz and Mendelsohn LLP to provide all legal services in connection with a $175 million mortgage 701financing with Nomura Asset Capital Corporation and Nomura Securities International, Inc. (Nomura mortgage financing) and a restructuring of ownership interests, all involving four major New York City office buildings and various interests in six other New York properties. The restructuring entailed the formation of numerous limited liability companies, the conversion of existing partnerships to limited liability companies and the transfer of real estate assets, partnership interests and membership interests to a number of these limited liability companies.

Those transactions were completed at the end of 1995. The legal work in planning, structuring, negotiating and preparing the necessary closing papers was, concededly, of very substantial complexity, for which the fees totaled approximately $1 million. The closing report alone consisted of some 14 volumes containing more than 550 documents.

In early 1996, petitioners and the Proskauer firm had a falling out. Petitioners then retained Nixon, Hargrave, Devans, & Doyle LLP, their present counsel, to represent them in connection with all matters related to the Nomura mortgage financing and the commercial real estate ownership restructuring. Nixon, Hargrave asked Proskauer to turn over its files in their entirety on the financing and restructuring matters, and tendered a check for Proskauer’s bindery expenses for those transactions, that being the only remaining outstanding claim of Proskauer for payment with respect to services and disbursements arising out of those matters.

In addition to the closing report documents previously delivered, in the course of negotiations between the two firms during the spring of 1996, Proskauer also turned over additional documents from its files consisting of client-supplied papers, client correspondence and what could be characterized as supporting closing papers such as appraisals, tax forms, formal legal opinions and environmental and engineering reports. The firm also furnished a 58-page index of its files on the Sage Realty transactions obtained from its records department’s computerized file management program. Proskauer refused, however, to turn over a large number of items identified in the index such as internal legal memoranda, drafts of instruments, mark-ups, notes on contracts and transactions and ownership structure charts. Petitioners claim that Proskauer also failed to turn over firm correspondence with third parties and conference negotiation notes.

This special proceeding was then commenced by petitioners to recover all of the outstanding papers in the Proskauer files relating to Proskauer’s representation on the foregoing real estate financing and restructuring matters. The petition alleges that, although the Nomura mortgage financing and commercial real estate ownership restructuring may have culminated in a closing, there remain outstanding complex financial and tax reporting obligations of petitioners requiring legal guidance from their present counsel. In subsequent affidavits, Nixon, Hargrave averred that 702the underlying documents, such as drafts and transaction charts, are needed for complete understanding of how certain provisions in the various legal instruments were finally negotiated and to assess the full extent of petitioners’ ongoing compliance obligations. Proskauer’s response was that all third-party correspondence and all documents provided by petitioners in relation to these transactions had been delivered and that those papers, together with the previously delivered closing binder containing all closing instruments, supporting documents and summaries of contents, were amply sufficient to enable present counsel to advise petitioners on their continuing obligations. Proskauer refused to make any further general transfer of its files on the represented matters, albeit expressing willingness to entertain a particularized request upon a showing of need.

\[The\] Supreme Court, relying upon Zackiva Communications Corp. v. Milberg Weiss Bershad Specthrie & Lerach, accepted Proskauer’s position that petitioners were not entitled to more from the firm’s files than the closing binder documents and their own client papers, all of which had previously been furnished by that firm. The Appellate Division affirmed. That Court held that as to the “concluded business financing and restructuring matters,” the Proskauer files at issue, the firm’s “drafts, internal memoranda, mark-ups, research” and other internal documents containing “ ‘the opinions, reflections and thought processes’ ” of counsel were Proskauer’s “private property,” which need not be furnished to petitioners absent a showing of particularized need. We granted petitioners leave to appeal, and now reverse.

A majority of courts and State legal ethics advisory bodies considering a client’s access to the attorney’s file in a represented matter, upon termination of the attorney-client relationship, where no claim for unpaid legal fees is outstanding, presumptively accord the client full access to the entire attorney’s file on a represented matter with narrow exceptions. \* \* \*

The American Law Institute, in its Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers essentially embraced the majority position (see, Restatement \[Third\] of Law Governing Lawyers § 58 \[Proposed Final Draft No. 1, 1996\]). The draft Restatement provides that a former client is to be accorded access to “inspect and copy any documents possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds exist to refuse”. Even without a request, an attorney is obligated to deliver to the client, not later than promptly after representation ends, “such originals and copies of other documents possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation as the \[former\] client reasonably needs”.

By contrast, a minority (although a substantial number) of courts and State bar legal ethics authorities, including the Appellate Division in this case and in Zackiva Communications Corp. v Milberg Weiss Bershad Specthrie & Lerach, supra, distinguish between the “end product” of an attorney’s 703services, the documents representing which belong to the client, and the attorney’s “work product” leading to the creation of those end product documents, which remains the property of the attorney. \* \* \*

End product, under the foregoing minority view, includes such items as pleadings actually filed in an action; correspondence with a client, opposing counsel and witnesses; and other papers “exposed to public light by the attorney to further \[the\] client’s interests”; and the final versions of contracts, wills, corporate records and similar records prepared for the client’s actual use. The attorney’s work product, to which the client is not entitled access, includes all preliminary documents “used by the lawyer to reach the end result,” such as internal legal memoranda and preliminary drafts of pleadings and legal instruments. As to these and similar documents, the minority view is that the client is only entitled to access to the extent of a demonstrated need in order to understand the end product documents, with the burden of justification on the client.

We conclude that the majority position, as adopted in the final draft of the American Law Institute Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers, represents the sounder view. First, an expansive general right of the client to the contents of the attorney’s file, upon termination of the attorney-client relationship, more closely conforms to the position taken by the courts of this State on the client’s broad rights to the contents of the file when representation ceases on a matter still pending. An “attorney’s work product” exception has been rejected in that context.

Moreover, when the attorney’s file is sought in connection with a pending matter, courts also have refused to recognize a property right of the attorney in the file superior to that of the client. We can discern no principled basis upon which exclusive property rights to an attorney’s work product in a client’s file spring into being in favor of the attorney at the conclusion of a represented matter. Indeed, this case illustrates that, often, no unequivocal line can be drawn between pending and completed legal matters; hence, the continued likelihood of useful reference to work product materials in the client’s file.

Second, the minority position adopted by the courts below unrealistically and, in our view, unfairly places the burden on the client to demonstrate a need for specific work product documents in the attorney’s file on the represented matter. Again, this case is illustrative that in a complex transaction where the file may be voluminous (commensurably increasing the likely usefulness of work product materials to advise the client concerning ongoing rights and obligations), the client’s need for access to a particular paper cannot be demonstrated except in the most general terms, in the absence of prior disclosure of the content of the very document to which access is sought. The attorney in possession of the contents of the file is in a far better position to demonstrate that a particular document 704would furnish no useful purpose in serving the client’s present needs for legal advice.

Affording the client presumptive access to the attorney’s entire file on the represented matter, subject to narrow exceptions, is also supported, although not necessarily dictated, by the lawyer’s ethical obligations arising out of representation in a given matter. As we recognized in Tekni-Plex, Inc. v. Meyner & Landis, an attorney’s fiduciary relationship with a client may continue even after representation has concluded. Among the duties of an attorney as a fiduciary and agent of the client are those of openness and conscientious disclosure. As we remarked in another context, equally applicable here, “\[s\]ince the reign of Elizabeth I, the law has as a matter of policy encouraged full disclosure between attorney and client” That obligation of forthrightness of an attorney toward a client is not furthered by the attorney’s ability to cull from the client’s file documents generated through fully compensated representation, which the attorney unilaterally decides the client has no right to see.

Thus, we conclude that the courts below erred in restricting petitioners’ access to the Proskauer files on the firm’s representation in the instant financing and real estate ownership restructuring matters essentially to end product documents. Barring a substantial showing by the Proskauer firm of good cause to refuse client access, petitioners should be entitled to inspect and copy work product materials, for the creation of which they paid during the course of the firm’s representation.

Proskauer, however, should not be required to disclose documents which might violate a duty of nondisclosure owed to a third party, or otherwise imposed by law. Additionally, nonaccess would be permissible as to firm documents intended for internal law office review and use. “The need for lawyers to be able to set down their thoughts privately in order to assure effective and appropriate representation warrants keeping such documents secret from the client involved.” This might include, for example, documents containing a firm attorney’s general or other assessment of the client, or tentative preliminary impressions of the legal or factual issues presented in the representation, recorded primarily for the purpose of giving internal direction to facilitate performance of the legal services entailed in that representation. Such documents presumably are unlikely to be of any significant usefulness to the client or to a successor attorney. Upon remittal, which will be required in the instant case, disputes concerning access to these and other categories of internal law firm papers will be resolved in the first instance by Supreme Court through a hearing which might necessitate in camera review. Moreover, Proskauer can apply to that court for protective remedies in the event of oppression or harassment in connection with demands for file inspection, delivery of original documents or reproduction.

705 

We also conclude that, as a general proposition, unless a law firm has already been paid for assemblage and delivery of documents to the client, performing that function is properly chargeable to the client under customary fee schedules of the firm, or pursuant to the terms of any governing retainer agreement.

Finally, we caution that our holding in this matter is not to be construed as altering any existing standard of professional responsibility or generally accepted practice concerning a lawyer’s duty to retain and safeguard all or portions of a client’s file once a matter is concluded. The dispute here is solely over client access to the specific files which, in fact, were retained following the termination of Proskauer’s representation.

Accordingly, the order of the Appellate Division should be reversed, with costs, and the matter remitted to Supreme Court for further proceedings not inconsistent with this opinion.

Questions

1.Recall our discussion of information as property in Chapter 1. How does the Court conceive the property interest here?

2.How does privacy play a role in this dispute?

3.Do you think that this decision strikes the right balance between an attorney’s information interests and those of the client?

E.Document Retention and Destruction

The question of ownership of information and documents related to a lawyer’s or law firm’s representation of a client can have significant ramifications for document retention and destruction policies (discussed in Chapter 12) that are an essential part of any IG plan. Obviously, to the extent information and documents are owned by the client, and not the lawyer or law firm, then it is the client who should determine whether and when to destroy those materials. This decision must be governed by the client’s legal obligations and business considerations, including applicable litigation hold rules as discussed in Chapter 13.

However, even if certain information and documents are technically “owned” by a client, lawyers and law firms often have an interest in maintaining the originals and copies of those materials. For instance, it is not uncommon for a client to retain a law firm to be the repository of certain of its records, like corporate records and trademark registration files. Also, lawyers and law firms often keep copies of client files in case they are accused of malpractice or other wrongdoing. In fact, malpractice insurance providers typically require the retention of client files for specified periods of time, depending upon the nature of the legal work provided.

706 

Aside from legal considerations, whether documents that are generated in the course of representing a client are retained or destroyed often depends upon the scope and nature of the representation. If the representation ends, then typically all or some portion of the client file will be returned to the client or transferred to the client’s new attorneys, in which case a lawyer or law firm might only keep copies of the files for malpractice purposes and they can be destroyed once the statute of limitation on a malpractice claim expires. However, depending upon the nature of the representation, the applicable statutes of limitations may not begin to run for years or decades, thereby requiring some law firms to retain client files for lengthy periods of time. For instance, estate planning lawyers frequently keep the originals, or at least copies, of the wills and trusts they prepare for clients. Also, lawyers and law firms often have ongoing relationships with clients that justify the retention of client files for long periods of time.

While the particulars of each state’s laws regarding the ownership and definition of client files may differ, the Restatement (Third) of the Law Governing Lawyers, provides guidance concerning the handling of the information deemed to be the property of the client, as follows:

Restatement (Third) of Law Governing Lawyers (2000)

§ 45 Surrendering Possession of Property

(1)Except as provided in Subsection (2), a lawyer must promptly deliver, to the client or nonclient so entitled, funds or other property in the lawyer’s possession belonging to a client or nonclient.

(2)A lawyer may retain possession of funds or other property of a client or nonclient if:

(a)the client or nonclient consents;

(b)the lawyer’s client is entitled to the property, the lawyer appropriately possesses the property for purposes of the representation, and the client has not asked for delivery of the property;

(c)the lawyer has a valid lien on the property (see § 43);

(d)there are substantial grounds for dispute as to the person entitled to the property; or

(e)delivering the property to the client or nonclient would violate a court order or other legal obligation of the lawyer.

§ 46 Documents Relating to a Representation

(1)A lawyer must take reasonable steps to safeguard documents in the lawyer’s possession relating to the representation of a client or former client.

707 

(2)On request, a lawyer must allow a client or former client to inspect and copy any document possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation, unless substantial grounds exist to refuse.

(3)Unless a client or former client consents to nondelivery or substantial grounds exist for refusing to make delivery, a lawyer must deliver to the client or former client, at an appropriate time and in any event promptly after the representation ends, such originals and copies of other documents possessed by the lawyer relating to the representation as the client or former client reasonably needs.

(4)Notwithstanding Subsections (2) and (3), a lawyer may decline to deliver to a client or former client an original or copy of any document under circumstances permitted by § 43(1) \[the provision concerning lawyer liens\].

———

If the representation of a client does not end and is ongoing, then the decision to retain or destroy client files often depends upon whether a specific matter has been concluded. See ABA Model Rule of Professional Conduct, Rule 1.15 (a). Critical to this issue is the question of when representation is terminated. Moreover, legal and contractual obligations and practical concerns may require that the subject documents be retained for longer than the law or applicable rule of professional conduct requires. For instance, the rules of professional conduct of some states have extended the prescribed retention period specified in the ABA Model Rules of Professional Conduct from five to six or seven years. See, e.g., N.C. R. Prof. C. 1.15-3(g) (six years); Ohio R. Prof. C. 1.15(a) (seven years). Also, litigation hold rules (discussed in Chapter 13) often require the suspension of applicable document destruction policies and timelines for as long as it takes for the litigation to conclude.

Given the foregoing considerations, it is often easier and less costly for a business, including lawyers and law firms, to retain rather than destroy records. But while there are potential adverse consequences associated with the premature destruction of records, there are also costs and risks associated with their retention past the date when they are legally or contractually required to be retained. Most obvious is the cost of storage, whether the documents exist in tangible or digital form. This includes the cost of creating and maintaining an inventory of documents and safeguarding and securing the physical and virtual places where the documents are stored.

A less obvious concern relates to the information that the documents might reveal about the potential liability or culpability of a client or its lawyers. As previously noted, there are legal and ethical obligations that preclude the destruction of documents and evidence, but generally, 708business records and client files do not need to be kept forever. Thus, a best practice of IG is for businesses to adopt a policy and schedule for the regular destruction of information unless legal or business considerations suggest otherwise.

Notes

1.Waiving privilege through careless practice. The recurring nightmare for a litigation attorney is the risk of accidentally waiving a client’s privilege through error or careless practice. The fast-paced nature of many attorneys’ practices today makes the risk of such an event even more likely. Errant email communications are a particular risk. See, e.g., Latele Television, C.A. v. Telemundo Commc’ns Grp., LLC, 2014 WL 4449451 (S.D. Fla. Sept. 10, 2014) (holding that by inadvertently forwarding several email strings and attachments to a nonparty, plaintiff’s attorney waived attorney-client privilege as to 132 pages of emails); Kilopass Tech. Inc. v. Sidense Corp. (N.D. Cal. 2012) 2012 WL 1534065 at 2–3 (attorney-client privilege deemed waived as to privileged documents released through e-discovery because screening procedures employed were unreasonable); Curto v. Med. World Commc’ns, Inc., 783 F. Supp. 2d 373 (E.D.N.Y. 2011) (holding that plaintiff’s attorney waived attorney-client privilege when he filed his confidential memoranda on court’s publicly-accessible electronic docket while also serving copies of the memoranda on Defendant’s attorney).

Four practical tips: (1) turn-off “Reply All” or your email and disable “Reply All” for all emails that you send; (2) compose emails before filling in the “to” line of the email, and then carefully select the recipient(s) of the email; (3) do not send a “copy” of emails to too many people, if any; and (4) frequently update and limit your list of email addresses.

2.Redaction and sealing errors. Today’s information technology ecosystem finds lawyers increasingly vulnerable to waiving confidentiality and privilege through failed technological redaction. (See Chapter 13 for a discussion of redaction and sealing during litigation; generally, it cannot be done without a court order or the agreement of opposing counsel.) For example, a high-profile error involved Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s criminal investigation into former Campaign Chairman for President Donald J. Trump, Paul Manafort. Manafort’s attorneys had redacted portions of a response to Mueller’s allegations that Manafort had breached a criminal plea agreement, but according to The Hill, “court watchers were able to view the filing in its entirety by copying and pasting the redacted sections.” Morgan Chalfant, Manafort suspected of sharing polling data with associate linked to Russian intelligence, The Hill, January 8, 2019. Needless to say, attorneys need to guard against such errors, take their time when handling confidential and privileged information, and take IG seriously.
